docs.title: Tashtiot APIs Library
docs.text:
A unified Python package that bundles two largely independent toolsets for building production-ready services:

  1. Infrastructure connectors — async clients for AWX (Ansible Tower), ArgoCD, Bitbucket Server ("Git"), and HashiCorp Vault. Each validates responses, returns typed Pydantic models, and raises typed exceptions.
  2. FastAPI template — a reusable application factory (general_create_app) with built-in middleware, Prometheus metrics, health probes, self-hosted Swagger, structured Loguru logging, inbound JWT auth, outbound SSO, and a Remote Config API capability.

You pip install the package and import from the top-level tashtiot_apis_library namespace — there is no app to "run" here, the library is the product.

pip install tashtiot-apis-library

from tashtiot_apis_library import AWX, ArgoCD, Git, Vault, general_create_app

docs.title: How this documentation is organised
docs.text:
These docs follow the Diátaxis framework — four sections, each answering a different need. Start in the corner that matches what you're trying to do:

  • Tutorials

    Learning-oriented. Hands-on lessons that take you from zero to a working, secured app.

  • How-to guides

    Task-oriented. Focused recipes for a specific goal — read a file from Bitbucket, call a service with SSO, enable the Remote Config API.

  • Reference

    Information-oriented. The dry facts: every environment variable, the CLI flags, and the auto-generated API reference for every public symbol.

  • Explanation

    Understanding-oriented. The "why" — the architecture, the auth design, and how logging works.

Working on the library rather than with it? See Contributing for the dev setup, tooling, and conventions.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
You want to… Go to Build a company API the standard way Reference: API standards Stand up a FastAPI service in minutes Tutorial: Your first app Protect endpoints with JWT bearer auth Tutorial: Secure your API Talk to ArgoCD / AWX / Vault / Bitbucket How-to: connectors Authenticate outbound calls to other services How-to: Call services with SSO Look up an environment variable Reference: Configuration Understand the connector pattern Explanation: Architecture

Requirements

Python ≥ 3.10. The package depends on FastAPI, httpx, Pydantic v2, Loguru, and PyJWT; the heavy auth and caching dependencies are imported lazily, so features you don't use cost nothing at import time.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: This section is for people working on the library (extending it, fixing it, releasing it), as opposed to consuming it. If you're using the package, start with the Tutorials.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
• Development — set up your environment with uv, run the tests, the linter (Ruff), and the type checker (ty), and build the docs.
  • Architecture — the two toolsets, the three-layer connector pattern, and the public-surface / _internal boundary you should respect.
  • Logging — the Loguru conventions new code should follow.
  • Extending the library:
    • Add a new connector — the models → client → service pattern.
    • Extend the FastAPI template — add a middleware, route, or utility.

docs.title: House rules in one paragraph
docs.text:
Use relative imports within the package; keep the connector three-layer split; return typed Pydantic models and raise typed errors (never raw dicts/HTTP codes); log with from loguru import logger at the standard levels; and keep new public symbols on the narrow public surface (utils / auth / security / errors), with implementation under _internal/. Run Ruff + the tests before opening a PR — see Development.

Maintainer-only concerns (owners, the release/publish process) live in the repo's MAINTAINERS.md.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: How to set up a working environment and run the project's checks. The toolchain is Astral's: uv (environment + runner), Ruff (lint + format), and ty (type check).

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
uv is used as a fast runner — there is no committed uv.lock. This is a library, so consumers resolve against the dependency ranges in pyproject.toml; a lockfile would only pin our own dev environment and churn against the setuptools-scm version. Plain pip works too.

uv venv                              # create .venv
uv pip install -e ".[dev,docs]"      # dev tools + docs toolchain
# equivalently, without uv:
#   python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install -e ".[dev,docs]"

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
The suite lives in the top-level tests/ tree and runs from the repo root:

uv run pytest                                         # whole suite (with coverage)
uv run pytest tests/connectors/test_awx_client.py     # one file

docs.title: Lint & format (Ruff)
docs.text:
uv run ruff format .          # format
uv run ruff check . --fix     # lint, auto-fixing what it safely can

Ruff config is in pyproject.toml ([tool.ruff]). The rule set is intentionally conservative; UP (pyupgrade), TID252 (it would ban the package's relative imports), and G (the codebase mixes f-string and {}-style Loguru calls) are deliberately not enabled.

docs.title: Type check (ty)
docs.text:
uv run ty check src           # advisory — scoped to the shipped package

ty is advisory / non-blocking: it's beta and has no Pydantic plugin yet, so it reports a known baseline of mostly Optional-annotation and Pydantic false positives. Treat it as a signal, not a gate.

docs.title: Pre-commit hooks
docs.text:
uv run pre-commit install                                  # enable on every commit
uv run pre-commit run --all-files                          # run ruff + ruff-format now
uv run pre-commit run ty --hook-stage manual --all-files   # run the advisory ty hook

ruff and ruff-format run on every commit; ty is a manual-stage hook so its beta noise never blocks a commit.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
The docs you're reading are built with MkDocs (Material) + mkdocstrings:

uv run mkdocs serve            # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
uv run mkdocs build --strict   # what CI-equivalent checks expect: fails on any broken link

The API reference pages are generated from docstrings, so keep docstrings accurate when you change public signatures.

docs.title: Before you open a PR
docs.text:
• uv run ruff format . && uv run ruff check . — clean.
  • uv run pytest — green.
  • uv run mkdocs build --strict — clean, if you touched docs or public docstrings.

CI (.woodpecker/check.yaml) runs Ruff + pytest + advisory ty on every push/PR.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
Explanation is understanding-oriented: it discusses the why behind the library — the design decisions, the structure, and the trade-offs. Read these when you want context, not a step-by-step (that's the How-to guides) or a lookup (that's the Reference).

  • Architecture — the two independent toolsets, the three-layer connector pattern, and the public-surface / _internal boundary.
  • Authentication design — the dual-gate, the three verification modes plus OIDC discovery, inbound vs outbound, and why PyJWT is imported lazily.
  • Dynamic config validation — where each coordinate/config check lives, and why config-dependent fields are validated in a dependency, not a Pydantic validator.
  • OpenAPI & Swagger injection — OpenAPI/Swagger basics and how the library patches the generated schema so Swagger shows live coordinate dropdowns.
  • Logging — how a single global Loguru logger is configured once at import and shared everywhere.
  • Async and the event loop — what async is, why the library uses it instead of a sync design, and why blocking calls are banned.
  • Job queues & long-running work — the job-queue concept, why AWX already is one, and the options when your API needs its own.
  • Cloud-native APIs & multiple replicas — what running several identical pods means for state, idempotency, background tasks, shutdown, rollouts and observability.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page explains how the package is organised and why.

docs.title: Two independent toolsets, one package
docs.text:
The library ships two largely independent toolsets under one distribution:

  1. Infrastructure connectors (connectors/) — async clients for ArgoCD, AWX, Bitbucket Server, and Vault.
  2. FastAPI template (fastapi_template/) — the general_create_app application factory and its middleware, metrics, probes, auth, and Remote Config capability.

They're bundled together for convenience, but a consumer can use either alone. The one dependency direction between them: connectors depend on fastapi_template.utils.BaseAPI (the shared outbound HTTP wrapper), so the FastAPI template is a dependency of the connectors, not the reverse.

docs.title: The three-layer connector pattern
docs.text:
Every connector under connectors/<name>/ is split into exactly three modules, and new ones must follow suit (see Add a new connector):

Layer File Responsibility Models models.py Pydantic request/response shapes. Aliases for camelCase JSON; tolerate unknown fields. Client client.py Low-level HTTP via BaseAPI. Converts error status codes into typed exceptions; returns parsed models, never raw dicts. Service service.py The high-level class users instantiate (AWX, Git, …). Composes the client and adds orchestration: polling, wait_for_*, retries.

Adding a capability means touching the layers bottom-up: model (if new shapes) → client method → service method.

The FastAPI template's outbound-SSO area follows the same model/logic split — its Pydantic data models (SSOConfig, TokenResponse) live in a co-located _internal/security/models.py, while the client/auth classes stay in _internal/security/sso.py.

docs.title: Standardized responses and errors
docs.text: Service methods return OperationResponse subclasses (status, status_code, return_code, stdout) rather than raw API payloads — AWXOperationResponse adds job_id, ArgoOperationResponse adds app_name. Errors are a parallel hierarchy: ExternalServiceError(HTTPException) subclassed per connector (ArgoCDError, GitError, VaultError, AWXError). Because they extend fastapi.HTTPException, raising one inside a route surfaces directly as an HTTP response.

docs.title: The public surface vs _internal
docs.text:
The FastAPI template keeps a deliberately narrow public surface; everything under _internal/ is private implementation. The public modules are organised by concern, each a stable import home:

Module Concern fastapi_template general_create_app (+ lazy enable_remote_config_api) fastapi_template.utils infra utilities — BaseAPI, settings fastapi_template.auth inbound JWT — get_current_claims, JWTVerifier, verify_token, AuthMode, keygen fastapi_template.security outbound SSO — sso_authenticated_api, SSOConfig, StaticBearerAuth, … fastapi_template.errors the auth error types

These public modules are thin re-export facades over _internal. This split lets the heavy dependencies stay lazy (see Authentication design and Logging) and gives consumers a small, intention-revealing API to import from.

docs.title: Imports within the package
docs.text: Internal code uses relative imports (from .client import ..., from ..errors import ..., from ...fastapi_template.utils import BaseAPI). Absolute self-imports are avoided because the distribution name is rewritten at build time — an absolute self-import would be fragile.

docs.title: Async and the event loop
docs.text: Everything in this library is asynchronous: the connectors, the outbound SSO client, the Remote Config provider and the app factory's background tasks. This page explains what that means, why we chose it over a synchronous design, and why it forces the async rules in API standards.

docs.title: What "async" means
docs.text:
A normal (synchronous) program does one thing at a time. When it calls another service over the network, the thread blocks and does nothing until the reply arrives. To serve 50 requests at once, a sync server needs about 50 threads or processes, and most of them spend their time idle.

An asynchronous program runs on an event loop, a single thread that juggles many tasks. When a task reaches a slow I/O call and awaits it, the task hands control back to the loop. The loop then runs other tasks while the network or disk does its work, and resumes the first task when its result is ready.

# Sync: the thread is stuck for the full round-trip.
response = requests.get("https://awx/api/v2/jobs/42/")

# Async: while this request is in flight, the event loop serves other requests.
response = await client.get("/api/v2/jobs/42/")
Term Meaning async def Defines a coroutine function. Calling it returns a coroutine object; nothing runs until it is awaited or scheduled. await x "Pause me here until x finishes; let the loop run other things meanwhile." Only allowed inside async def. Event loop The scheduler that runs coroutines. uvicorn starts one per worker process. Task A coroutine scheduled on the loop (asyncio.create_task(...)) so it runs concurrently with others. Blocking call Anything that holds the thread without awaiting (time.sleep, requests.get, a sync DB driver, heavy CPU work).

Note

Async is concurrency, not parallelism. It overlaps waiting, not computing. One event loop still uses one CPU core.

docs.title: Why async instead of sync APIs
docs.text:
Our APIs are orchestrators. A typical request validates input, then calls AWX, ArgoCD, Vault, Bitbucket, the Config API or an SSO token endpoint, and returns. Almost all of the request time is spent waiting on other systems, which is the case async is built for.

  • Throughput per pod: One worker can hold hundreds of in-flight requests to slow back-ends without a thread for each, so we need fewer replicas and less memory.
  • Built-in fan-out: Independent calls can run at the same time with asyncio.gather, so the request takes as long as the slowest call instead of the sum of all calls.
  • Cheap waiting: await asyncio.sleep(5) inside a "wait for the AWX job" loop costs nothing. time.sleep(5) would block a whole worker.
  • Background work in-process: Startup tasks such as the Remote Config allowlist poller run on the same loop as the request handlers.
  • One model end to end: Mixing sync and async code forces thread hops and hides bugs. Being async everywhere keeps the model simple.

docs.title: How the library is async
docs.text:
• Every connector method is a coroutine. AWX, ArgoCD, Git and Vault expose only async def methods, so callers must await them (Architecture).
  • All outbound HTTP goes through BaseAPI, a thin wrapper that builds an httpx.AsyncClient. Used as async with BaseAPI(...) as client:, it closes its connection pool when the block ends.
  • Git uses subprocesses asynchronously. The Git connector runs git over SSH with asyncio.create_subprocess_exec, so even shelling out doesn't block the loop.
  • Waiting helpers poll with asyncio.sleep. AWX.wait_for_job_completion and ArgoCD.wait_for_app_creation are examples. A long wait costs a sleeping coroutine, not a thread.
  • Outbound SSO and Remote Config are async too. Token fetches and upstream config lookups are awaited, and their results are cached (Authentication design).
  • The app lifespan runs background coroutines. general_create_app launches every coroutine in app.state.async_background_tasks at startup and cancels them on shutdown.

docs.title: Consequences: why the rules exist
docs.text:
Because one thread serves every request on a worker, a single blocking call stalls all of them. A time.sleep(5) in one handler means no other request on that worker gets an answer for five seconds. This is the reason behind each of the async rules:

  • Sync I/O libraries are banned in async code. requests and sync DB drivers block the loop. The async equivalents (httpx, async drivers) yield back to it.
  • Blocking work you can't avoid goes to a thread with asyncio.to_thread. The loop then waits on the thread instead of being stuck inside the call.
  • Plain def handlers run in a thread pool. FastAPI runs them in a pool of about 40 threads by default so they don't block the loop. That is fine for trivial CPU-only handlers, but using it as a way to call sync I/O just moves the bottleneck to the pool.
  • Every network wait needs a timeout. An awaited call that never returns doesn't block other requests, but it holds its request open, and its connection, forever.
  • Tasks need a reference. The loop holds only a weak reference to a task created with asyncio.create_task, so an unreferenced task can be garbage-collected mid-run (see Job queues and long-running work).
  • Don't start a loop inside the app. asyncio.run() fails inside an already-running loop, and uvicorn already runs one.

docs.title: Authentication design
docs.text:
The library has two distinct auth concerns that are easy to conflate, so they're kept in separate public modules:

  • Inbound (fastapi_template.auth) — verifying bearer tokens on requests this service receives.
  • Outbound (fastapi_template.security) — obtaining bearer tokens to call other services.

This page explains the design behind both.

docs.title: Inbound: enforced by middleware, not dependencies
docs.text:
Inbound auth is enforced by an AuthMiddleware, not by per-route FastAPI dependencies. The middleware extracts a Bearer <token> from the configured header, verifies it, and stashes the claims on request.state.user; routes read them via Depends(get_current_claims). Doing it in middleware means every route is protected by default (minus an explicit exclude list), rather than relying on each route remembering to add a dependency.

A consequence: because the OpenAPI schema wouldn't otherwise carry security info, the library injects a global BearerAuth scheme so Swagger shows an Authorize button when auth is active.

docs.title: The dual-gate
docs.text:
Auth activates only when both are true:

  • the code flag enable_auth=True passed to general_create_app, and
  • the runtime switch AUTH_ENABLED=true in the environment.

Two gates make it impossible to accidentally ship auth-on code that runs auth-off (or vice versa) by changing only one of them. A deployment can also flip auth off at runtime without a code change.

docs.title: Verification modes
docs.text:
The verifier auto-selects exactly one mode from the configured material, and raises AuthConfigError at startup if zero or more than one is set (fail fast, not on first request):

Material Mode AUTH_HS256_SECRET HS256 — symmetric shared secret AUTH_PUBLIC_KEY_PEM / AUTH_PUBLIC_KEY_PATH LOCAL_PUBKEY — offline RS256 against a public key AUTH_JWKS_URL or AUTH_OIDC_ISSUER JWKS — RS256 against keys fetched from a JWKS endpoint

docs.title: OIDC discovery
docs.text: For any standards-compliant OIDC provider you can set AUTH_OIDC_ISSUER alone: at startup the library fetches the issuer's /.well-known/openid-configuration, discovers its jwks_uri, and verifies in JWKS mode. The issuer also becomes the default expected iss claim. An explicit AUTH_JWKS_URL always wins over discovery. (AUTH_JWKS_URL and AUTH_OIDC_ISSUER are treated as one material group, not two competing ones.)

docs.title: Non-expiring tokens
docs.text: The verifier requires an exp claim by default. Set AUTH_REQUIRE_EXP=false to accept tokens minted without one (e.g. dev tokens from gen-auth-material). A token that does carry exp is still validated, so expired tokens remain rejected either way.

docs.title: Outbound: client_credentials, cached and refreshed
docs.text:
Outbound SSO uses the OAuth2 client_credentials grant. The token client fetches a token, caches it, refreshes it shortly before expiry (AUTH_SSO_EXPIRY_SKEW), serialises concurrent refreshes with a lock, and the httpx.Auth retries once on a 401. Note that client_credentials issues no refresh token (RFC 6749 §4.4.3) — "refresh" means re-running the grant.

Server-side verification of SSO-issued tokens reuses JWKS mode: point AUTH_JWKS_URL at the provider's JWKS endpoint. So the inbound and outbound sides meet at JWKS.

docs.title: Why PyJWT is lazy
docs.text: PyJWT and cryptography are only needed when you actually verify or mint tokens. The public auth module serves its verifier/keygen names through a module-level __getattr__, and the _internal/security package __init__ is empty, so importing the package — or an auth-disabled app — never imports PyJWT. Consumers that only mint outbound tokens import from security, which pulls in the SSO code but not the inbound-JWT machinery. The cost of a feature is paid only when it's used.

docs.title: Cloud-native APIs and multiple replicas
docs.text: Our APIs run on Kubernetes (OpenShift) as several identical replicas of the same container. This page explains what that means for how an API is written, and why the API standards insist on stateless, idempotent code.

docs.title: What a replica is
docs.text:
A Deployment runs N pods from the same image. A Service in front of them spreads incoming requests across the pods:

                         ┌──▶ pod A  (uvicorn, one event loop, own memory)
client ──▶ Service / LB ─┼──▶ pod B  (uvicorn, one event loop, own memory)
                         └──▶ pod C  (uvicorn, one event loop, own memory)

The platform runs several replicas for:

  • Availability: a pod can die, be evicted or be rescheduled to another node at any moment, and the others keep serving.
  • Zero-downtime deploys: a rolling update replaces pods one at a time, so for a while the old and new versions run side by side.
  • Scale: more load means more pods, either set by hand or by an autoscaler.

The key fact: pods share nothing. Each has its own memory, its own event loop, its own filesystem and its own background tasks. Two consecutive requests from the same client can land on different pods.

docs.title: Keep state out of the process
docs.text:
Anything stored in a Python variable is visible to one pod only, and only until that pod restarts. So:

  • Don't keep the source of truth in memory. This covers job status, "in progress" flags, sessions, counters and anything a later request needs. A POST on pod A followed by a GET .../status on pod B must work. Status comes from the system that owns it (AWX, ArgoCD, Git, Vault) or from a shared store, which is why the job-queue page derives status from the external system.
  • Caches are fine, as long as they are only caches. The library caches SSO tokens, JWKS keys and Remote Config responses per pod. That is safe because a miss simply refetches. A cache must never hold the only copy of something.
  • The local filesystem is ephemeral and private to the pod. Don't write files that another request or a restart needs. Mounted read-only secrets (for example the Git SSH key) are fine.

docs.title: Expect the same work to arrive twice, on different pods
docs.text:
Clients and proxies retry, users double-click, and a request can time out on pod A and be retried on pod B. Two pods can also handle "create X" for the same name at the same moment.

  • Make operations idempotent: a repeated create, update or delete has the same end result (see API standards → Multi-step operations).
  • Use deterministic names, derived from the request, so a retry targets the same resource.
  • Let the external system arbitrate. An asyncio.Lock only serializes requests inside one pod, so it can't stop a race between two pods. Rely on the upstream's own conflict detection: the Git connector's add_file raises GitError with status 409 when the path already exists, and ArgoCD's create_app (with the default upsert=False) rejects an Application that already exists with a different spec. Translate those conflicts into 409.
  • Check-then-write is a race across replicas. "Read the secret, and if it is absent, write it" can interleave between two pods. Accept that, and keep the write itself idempotent, or move the guard into a system that offers an atomic operation.

docs.title: Background tasks run once per replica
docs.text:
Every coroutine in general_create_app(async_background_tasks=[...]) starts on every pod.

  • Read-only, idempotent loops are fine. The Remote Config allowlist poller runs N times, which just means N refreshes.
  • Work that must happen once ("clean up expired X every hour", "send the daily report") must not be an in-process loop, or it runs N times. Use something that runs once by design: a Kubernetes CronJob, an AWX schedule, or a job queue with a single consumer.
  • A task started with asyncio.create_task dies with its pod. A rolling update kills pods on purpose, so anything that must finish belongs in AWX or a job queue (Job queues and long-running work).

docs.title: Start fast, stop cleanly
docs.text:
Pods are started and stopped all the time, so both have to be cheap and safe:

  • Startup: configuration errors should fail fast, and they do: required settings and auth misconfiguration stop the app at creation. Heavy work doesn't belong at import time.
  • Shutdown: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits for the grace period (30 s by default), then kills the pod. uvicorn stops accepting connections and lets in-flight requests finish, and the library's lifespan cancels background tasks. Keep requests short (long work goes to a job), so they finish within the grace period.
  • Probes: /liveness answers "is the process alive?", and /readiness answers "should this pod get traffic?". The library serves both and excludes them from auth and request logging. They report the process only, not the upstreams. Don't make liveness depend on AWX or Vault, or an upstream outage would make Kubernetes restart every pod at once.

docs.title: Two versions run at the same time
docs.text:
During a rolling update, pods of version n and n+1 serve traffic together, and a client may hit both within one workflow.

  • Changes must be backward compatible for at least one release: new request fields are optional, and a response field isn't removed or renamed in place.
  • Breaking changes go in a new API version (/v2/...) next to the old one (API standards → Paths and versioning).
  • New background behaviour and new upstream writes must be safe while old pods are still running.

docs.title: Observability is per pod
docs.text:
• Logs go to stdout (the library configures Loguru that way). The platform collects them from every pod, so never write log files. Include identifiers (job_id, app_name, metadata.project) so one operation can be followed across pods.
  • Metrics at /metrics describe one pod. Prometheus scrapes each pod separately, so dashboards aggregate across pods (sum by (...)), and a per-pod counter on its own is not the API's total.

docs.title: Scale with replicas, not processes
docs.text: Run one uvicorn process per pod (as example-api's CMD does) and let Kubernetes add pods. Several worker processes inside one pod have the same no-shared-memory consequences as replicas, while hiding them from the platform's scheduling, probes and resource limits.

docs.title: Dynamic config validation
docs.text: The Remote Config capability validates a request's coordinates against values that change at runtime (the poller refreshes them from the upstream). Those checks live in two different places — some in the Pydantic model, some in a route dependency — and the split is deliberate. This page explains where each kind of check belongs and, in particular, why a field whose allowed values come from the resolved config must be validated in a dependency, not a Pydantic validator.

docs.title: Coordinate checks live in Pydantic validators
docs.text:
The coordinate values and their hierarchy are validated inside InfraMetadata, because everything they need is held in memory:

  • Each coordinate is checked against its live allowlist (LIVE_ALLOWED_*) by a field_validator.
  • The parent/child combination is checked against the live coordinate tree (LIVE_COORDINATE_TREE) by a model_validator — e.g. an island must sit under the chosen region.

Both read module-level state that the background poller repopulates in place. They're cheap, synchronous, and side-effect-free, so a Pydantic validator is the natural home: the model can't be constructed with an invalid coordinate, anywhere it's constructed.

docs.title: Config-dependent fields do not
docs.text:
Some fields aren't validated against a fixed allowlist at all — their valid values depend on the config resolved for the request's own coordinates. For example, the OS templates available to a VM differ at every leaf of the enterprise config; the allowed set for os_template is whatever that specific leaf configures.

That check cannot be a Pydantic validator, for three concrete reasons:

  1. It needs async I/O. Resolving the value means await provider.resolve_infra_config(...), an upstream HTTP call. Pydantic v2 validators are synchronous — there is no async validation hook during model construction.
  2. It needs the provider. A validator has no handle on the RemoteConfigProvider, and FastAPI passes no context into model validation when it parses a request, so the provider can't reach the validator.
  3. Validation should stay pure. Models are constructed in tests, in serialization round-trips, and in internal code paths — none of which should trigger a network call. Keeping I/O out of validation keeps the model cheap and predictable.

So this kind of check belongs at the request boundary — a small FastAPI dependency (or a check in the route body) that the application writes, running after the model's own validators and resolving the config once per request.

The rule of thumb: validate against in-memory data in the model; validate against resolved config in a dependency.

docs.title: Job queues and long-running work
docs.text: Many of our operations take longer than an HTTP request should stay open: a playbook run, an ArgoCD rollout, a multi-step change across Git, Vault and ArgoCD. This page explains the job-queue concept, why AWX already gives you one, and what your options are when it doesn't fit. The resulting API contract is listed in API standards.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
A job queue separates accepting work from doing work:

 client ──POST──▶ API ──enqueue(job)──▶ [ QUEUE ] ──▶ worker(s) ──▶ the actual work
   ▲               │                                       │
   │          202 {job_id}                          update job state
   └──GET /status/{job_id}──▶ API ──read state──▶ [ JOB STORE ] ◀┘
  1. The API validates the request, records a job, pushes it to a queue, and immediately returns 202 Accepted with a job_id.
  2. One or more workers take jobs from the queue and do the slow work.
  3. The client polls GET .../status/{job_id} (or receives a callback) until the job reaches a terminal status, such as successful, failed or canceled.

Why this shape matters:

  • HTTP has time limits. Proxies, ingress and clients typically cut connections at 30–60 s. A playbook or an ArgoCD rollout can take minutes.
  • Durability: a job in a queue survives an API pod restart or deploy. A request handler or an in-memory task does not.
  • Back-pressure: a burst of 500 requests becomes 500 queued jobs worked through at a controlled rate. It does not become 500 simultaneous executions.
  • Retries: failed jobs can be retried without the client resubmitting.
  • Independent scaling: workers scale separately from the API, and any API replica can answer the status call.

Queues usually deliver a job at least once, so the same job can run twice. The work a job does must therefore be idempotent: running it twice has the same effect as running it once.

docs.title: AWX is already a job queue
docs.text:
AWX works exactly like a job queue. When an API calls awx.launch_job(...):

  • AWX records the job and returns a job_id immediately. The job is pending/waiting in AWX's own queue.
  • AWX's execution nodes act as the workers: they pick the job up and run it (running).
  • AWX stores the job state and output (successful / failed / error / canceled), and it survives restarts of your API.
  • Your API reads that state with awx.get_job_status(job_id), or streams output with awx.get_job_output(...).

So an API that launches AWX jobs and exposes a status route is already using a job queue. It doesn't need another one. The DNS module in example-api follows this pattern: POST /dns/ launches the job and returns its job_id, and GET /dns/status/{job_id} reads it back from AWX.

This is also why the connector's launch response says status="successful": AWX accepted the job into its queue, but the job isn't done yet. The status call maps AWX states to a status_code in the response body: pending/waiting/running → 202, successful → 200, failed/error/canceled → 500. Your status route still answers with HTTP 200: a failed job is a result the client asked for, not an error in your API.

ArgoCD behaves in a similar asynchronous way: you request a sync, ArgoCD reconciles in the background, and you poll get_app_status. The HAProxy module in example-api works like this.

docs.title: When you need your own queue
docs.text:
If the slow work runs inside your API, rather than in AWX or ArgoCD, and it must survive restarts, be retried or be rate-limited, you need a job queue of your own.

There is no job queue in the library (for now)

tashtiot-apis-library does not ship a job-queue implementation. A team that needs one must either implement it or use an external solution, such as a message broker with a task-queue library. Another option is to model the work as an AWX job or workflow, which gives you the queue for free.

Whichever option a team chooses, a working queue gives you:

  • Durable jobs that survive restarts.
  • A job id and a status that any API replica can read, so the API can keep the same 202 + GET .../status/{job_id} contract as the AWX case.
  • Retries for transient failures (timeouts, 5xx, 429), with backoff and a maximum number of attempts. Validation or permission errors won't succeed on retry, so they aren't retried.
  • A timeout per job.
  • Somewhere to keep failed jobs for inspection.

A worker is just another entry point into the same code. It builds the connectors once and calls the same operations.py functions the API would.

docs.title: In-process background tasks are not a queue
docs.text:
asyncio.create_task(...) (or FastAPI's BackgroundTasks) runs work after the response is sent, inside the API process. The HAProxy module in example-api does this for the ArgoCD wait and sync. It is fine for short, best-effort work, but it gives you none of the queue guarantees:

  • The task is lost on restart, deploy or OOM. Any rollback it would have run never happens, which can leave Git and Vault half-applied.
  • The task lives in one replica. A status route can't ask another replica about it, so status must come from the external systems. The HAProxy status route asks ArgoCD for this reason.
  • No retries, no back-pressure.
  • The loop holds only a weak reference to the task. If nothing else references it, it can be garbage-collected mid-run. Keep tasks in a set until they finish: 
    _background_tasks: set[asyncio.Task] = set()


def spawn(coro) -> None:
    task = asyncio.create_task(coro)
    _background_tasks.add(task)
    task.add_done_callback(_background_tasks.discard)
  • Nobody awaits the task, so an exception that isn't caught and logged inside it disappears.

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text: The work… Use Finishes in well under ~5 s Inline: await it in the request Runs as an AWX job (or an ArgoCD sync) AWX/ArgoCD as the queue: launch it, return 202 + the id, expose a status route Is short, best-effort, and acceptable to lose on restart (a notification, a cache warm-up) An in-process background task Is long, runs inside your API, and must not be lost, needs retries or must be rate-limited Your own job queue, either implemented by the team or an external solution Is periodic (a poller or sync loop) general_create_app(async_background_tasks=[...]). One copy runs per replica, so make it idempotent.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: The library logs with Loguru, everywhere — and does so through a single shared logger configured once. This page explains how that works and the conventions it follows.

docs.title: One global logger, configured at import
docs.text:
Unlike the standard library's logging (where each module fetches its own named logger), Loguru exports a single pre-instantiated logger object. Every module does:

from loguru import logger

…and they all bind the same object. Configuration doesn't create a new logger — it mutates that shared object's sinks. The library does this once, as an import side-effect, in _internal/utils/__init__.py:

logger_config = Logger(settings.LOG_LEVEL)

Logger.__init__ runs two steps (in _internal/utils/logger.py):

  • setup_loguru() — logger.remove() drops the default handler, then logger.add(sys.stdout, …) installs a single colored stdout sink with a custom formatter (which does smart source-location detection) at the configured level.
  • configure_uvicorn() — installs a UvicornHandler that bridges stdlib/uvicorn log records into the same Loguru sink, so framework logs and library logs share one stream.

Because this runs the first time anything imports fastapi_template._internal.utils (which nearly everything does, transitively), logging is configured before any request — or even before app wiring.

docs.title: Consequences worth knowing
docs.text:
• It's order-dependent, last-writer-wins. The configuration calls logger.remove(), which clears all sinks — including ones you added yourself before importing the library. If you want your own sink, add it after importing the package.
  • LOG_LEVEL is read once. The sink is added with level=settings.LOG_LEVEL a single time, so changing the variable after import has no effect — set LOG_LEVEL before the process starts.

docs.title: The level convention
docs.text:
The connectors are the most thoroughly-logged code and set the house style the rest of the library (including auth, SSO, and the Remote Config API) follows:

Level Used for INFO User-facing operations and state transitions DEBUG Internal reads, polling loops, cache decisions, key resolution WARNING Misconfiguration or degraded-but-recoverable behavior ERROR External-service failures — logged immediately before raising the typed error

A record may pass extra={"location": "..."} to override the displayed source label — the request logger uses "Request"/"Response", and the auth middleware uses "Auth".

docs.title: OpenAPI, Swagger, and dynamic enum injection
docs.text: The Remote Config capability makes Swagger show live dropdowns of the allowed coordinate values — values that change at runtime as the poller refreshes them. This page explains how that works, starting from OpenAPI/Swagger basics, because the mechanism is "patch the generated schema," not a FastAPI feature.

docs.title: OpenAPI vs Swagger UI
docs.text:
Two different things people conflate:

  • OpenAPI is a document — a JSON (or YAML) description of your API: its paths, each method's parameters / request body, and every shape described with JSON Schema. It's just data.
  • Swagger UI is a renderer — a JavaScript app that reads an OpenAPI document and draws the interactive docs (the "Try it out" forms, dropdowns, the "Schemas" catalog at the bottom). It knows nothing about your Python code; it only knows the JSON.

FastAPI introspects your routes + Pydantic models and builds the OpenAPI dict via get_openapi(...), caching it on the app:

  • app.openapi() — the callable that returns the document.
  • app.openapi_schema — the cache. Set it to None and the next app.openapi() rebuilds.
  • /openapi.json returns app.openapi(); Swagger UI at /docs fetches that and renders it.

docs.title: The shape that matters
docs.text:
{
  "paths": { "/config": { "get": {
      "parameters": [ { "name": "region", "in": "query",
                        "schema": { "type": "string" } } ],       // query/path params, inline
      "requestBody": { "content": { "application/json": {
                        "schema": { "$ref": "#/components/schemas/DNSRecordCreate" } } } } } } },
  "components": { "schemas": {                                     // every model, once, by name
      "DNSRecordCreate": { "properties": { "metadata": { "$ref": "#/components/schemas/InfraMetadata" } } },
      "InfraMetadata":   { "properties": { "region": { "anyOf": [{"type":"string"},{"type":"null"}] } } } } }
}
  • enum is what Swagger turns into a dropdown. No enum → free-text box.
  • Query/path params are written inline under each operation's parameters.
  • Bodies (and response models) are not inlined: the schema is a $ref into the single shared components.schemas entry, and models nest by $ref-ing each other.
  • Optional/nullable fields render as {"anyOf": [{"type":"string"}, {"type":"null"}]} — the string type is in a branch, not at the top level.

docs.title: Why we post-process the document
docs.text: The valid coordinate values are dynamic (the poller refreshes LIVE_ALLOWED_* at runtime). A normal Pydantic Enum/Literal is frozen at import, so it can't track them. Instead the library patches the generated OpenAPI document every time it's built, writing the current allowlist values in as enum. That's the injection.

docs.title: The mechanism (make_config_openapi)
docs.text:
enable_remote_config_api installs it: app.openapi = make_config_openapi(app, coordinate_paths).

  • Wrap, don't replace. It captures the previous app.openapi and calls it. This matters because general_create_app already wrapped app.openapi to add the Bearer "Authorize" scheme; wrapping composes (enum wrapper → bearer wrapper → FastAPI), replacing would drop the Authorize button.
  • Live values by reference. It captures the LIVE_ALLOWED_* sets; the poller mutates them in place, so the captured references always see current values.
  • Regex path match. Each coordinate_paths entry is a regex fullmatched against every route path.
  • _inject is name-matched: only fields named after a coordinate (space/network/…) get an enum, and only when that allowlist is non-empty. It places the enum inside the anyOf string branch for Optional fields (where Swagger's model renderer looks) and top-level for flat ones.
  • Recursion. For bodies it descends through nested $ref components (so DNSRecordCreate → metadata: InfraMetadata → region works), with a visited-set cycle guard.
  • Refresh. The poller nulls app.openapi_schema each cycle, so the next /openapi.json request rebuilds + re-patches with the latest values — no restart.
  • Log. One INFO line names the routes that received values (once per change), which doubles as a "did my coordinate_paths match?" check.

docs.title: Why query params and bodies behave differently (the subtle bit)
docs.text:
OpenAPI represents the two kinds of input differently, and it shows up in Swagger:

  • A body / response model is a single object in components.schemas, referenced by $ref. The "Try it out" body form and the bottom "Schemas" section both render that same object. Patch it once → both show the enums.
  • Query params are inlined copies of each field into the operation's parameters list — there is no shared component for "a bag of query params." Patching the inlined copy makes the dropdown work, but the standalone InfraMetadata component (present because response models $ref it) is a different object the params don't point to.

So for query-param usage the injector patches the inlined params (dropdown works), and additionally patches the shared component for the dynamic models (InfraMetadata / RequiredInfraMetadata) so the "Schemas" section shows the options too. That component pass is scoped by name — the static MetadataRequest shares the field names but is intentionally not dynamic, so it's left untouched.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Name-matched and additive. A field must be named after a coordinate to get a dropdown; a mistyped path, non-coordinate field, or empty allowlist just yields nothing (hence the INFO log).
  • coordinate_paths is fullmatched. Use .* for partials; a non-matching entry is a silent no-op.
  • Components are shared. Patching a component (body/response models, and the named dynamic-model pass) shows the enums everywhere that component is $ref'd — one source of truth, not route-specific.

docs.title: Add a new connector
docs.text: This guide is for contributors extending the library with a new infrastructure connector. Connectors follow a strict three-layer pattern so they stay consistent and portable; new ones must match it.

docs.title: The three layers
docs.text:
Create a package under src/tashtiot_apis_library/connectors/<name>/ with exactly three modules:

connectors/<name>/
  models.py     # Pydantic request/response models
  client.py     # low-level HTTP
  service.py    # high-level class users instantiate

docs.title: 1. models.py — shapes
docs.text: Pydantic models for requests and responses. Use Field(alias="...") for camelCase JSON keys and model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow") to tolerate unknown fields. Connector-specific response subclasses of OperationResponse live here too (e.g. add a job_id).

docs.title: 2. client.py — low-level HTTP
docs.text:
Builds its httpx.AsyncClient via BaseAPI(...).client, converts HTTP error status codes into your typed exception, and returns parsed Pydantic models — never raw dicts.

from ...fastapi_template.utils import BaseAPI  # relative import — see below
from ..errors import MyServiceError
from .models import MyModel

docs.title: 3. service.py — high-level orchestration
docs.text: The class users instantiate (e.g. MyService). It composes the client (does not inherit it) and adds orchestration — polling, wait_for_*_completion, retries. Service methods generally return standardized OperationResponse subclasses rather than raw API models.

docs.title: Conventions to follow
docs.text:
• Relative imports only. Within the package use from ..errors import ..., from .models import ..., from ...fastapi_template.utils import BaseAPI. Absolute self-imports (from tashtiot_apis_library...) are incorrect here — they break portability (the package name is rewritten at build time).
  • Typed errors. Add MyServiceError(ExternalServiceError) to connectors/errors.py; the client raises it on status_code >= 400. Because ExternalServiceError extends fastapi.HTTPException, raising one inside a route surfaces directly as an HTTP response.
  • Standard logging. from loguru import logger; INFO for user-facing operations, DEBUG for internal reads/polling, ERROR before raising on external failures. See Logging.
  • Export it. Add the service and error to the relevant __init__.py and to the top-level tashtiot_apis_library/__init__.py __all__.

Adding a capability to an existing connector is the same idea bottom-up: model (if new shapes) → client method → service method.

docs.title: Call other services with SSO
docs.text:
When your service needs to call another protected service, use the outbound SSO helpers. They obtain a bearer token via the OAuth2 client_credentials grant, cache it, refresh it before expiry, and retry once on a 401.

These helpers live in tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.security, deliberately separate from the inbound-JWT machinery so a client-only consumer never pulls in PyJWT.

docs.title: The simple case: settings-driven
docs.text:
Configure the AUTH_SSO_* environment variables (see Configuration) and use sso_authenticated_api. Every request through the returned client carries a fresh token:

from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.security import sso_authenticated_api

async with sso_authenticated_api("https://downstream.example.com") as client:
    resp = await client.get("/protected")  # Authorization: Bearer <auto-managed>

docs.title: Several upstreams with different identities
docs.text:
To call multiple upstreams that each need a different identity or audience — independently of the AUTH_SSO_* singleton — pass an explicit SSOConfig. Build one per remote and reuse it so its token cache is shared:

from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.security import SSOConfig, sso_authenticated_api

billing = SSOConfig(
    token_url="https://idp/oauth/token",
    client_id="my-svc",
    client_secret="…",
    audience="https://billing.example.com",
)

async with sso_authenticated_api("https://billing.example.com", config=billing) as client:
    resp = await client.get("/invoices")

docs.title: A fixed, long-lived token
docs.text:
For an upstream secured by a static service token (no token endpoint), use StaticBearerAuth with any client that accepts an httpx.Auth — including the library's BaseAPI:

from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.security import StaticBearerAuth
from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.utils import BaseAPI

async with BaseAPI("https://downstream.example.com", auth=StaticBearerAuth("token")) as client:
    resp = await client.get("/protected")

docs.title: Just the raw token
docs.text:
from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.security import get_sso_token_client

token = await get_sso_token_client().get_token()
headers = await get_sso_token_client().auth_header()  # {"Authorization": "Bearer …"}

docs.title: Setting the downstream audience (aud)
docs.text:
How the downstream's aud claim is populated is provider-specific — it's decided when the token is minted at the token endpoint, not at the call site:

  • Auth0-style providers honour a request parameter: set AUTH_SSO_AUDIENCE and it is sent as the audience form field; the IdP stamps it into aud.
  • Keycloak ignores the audience parameter. Configure an Audience protocol mapper on a client scope, then request that scope via AUTH_SSO_SCOPE so the issued token carries the right aud. The downstream then validates it via its inbound AUTH_AUDIENCE.

No refresh token

client_credentials issues no OAuth2 refresh token (RFC 6749 §4.4.3). "Refresh" here means re-running the grant to mint a new access token when the cached one nears expiry.

docs.title: Constrain a field by resolved config
docs.text:
Sometimes a request field's valid values depend on the config resolved for the request's own coordinates — e.g. the OS templates a VM may use differ at every leaf of the enterprise config. The library deliberately doesn't ship a helper for this (the config key, the field, and the request model are all app-specific). Instead, write a small FastAPI dependency in your app. Here's the pattern.

For why this is a dependency rather than a Pydantic validator, see Dynamic config validation.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
from fastapi import Depends
from fastapi.exceptions import RequestValidationError
from pydantic import BaseModel

from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.config_api import RequiredInfraMetadata


class VMSpec(BaseModel):
    os_template: str
    instance_size: str


class VMRequest(BaseModel):
    metadata: RequiredInfraMetadata  # coordinates — validated against the allowlists + tree
    spec: VMSpec  # the fields whose allowed values depend on the config


def constrain_vm(provider):
    async def dependency(req: VMRequest) -> VMRequest:
        # The coordinate + spec models were already validated when the body was parsed.
        # Resolve the config for THIS request's coordinates, then check each field.
        config = await provider.resolve_infra_config(req.metadata)
        errors = []
        for field, config_key in (
            ("os_template", "os_templates"),
            ("instance_size", "instance_sizes"),
        ):
            value = getattr(req.spec, field)
            allowed = config.get(config_key) or []
            if allowed and value not in allowed:  # permissive when the config is unset/empty
                errors.append(
                    {
                        "type": "value_error",
                        "loc": ("body", "spec", field),  # points clients at the offending field
                        "msg": f"'{value}' is not permitted for the selected coordinates; "
                        f"allowed: {sorted(allowed)}",
                        "input": value,
                    }
                )
        if errors:
            raise RequestValidationError(errors)  # -> a standard 422, one entry per field
        return req

    return dependency


@app.post("/vms")
async def create_vm(
    req: VMRequest = Depends(constrain_vm(provider)),
): ...  # req is fully validated: coordinates AND spec.os_template / spec.instance_size

provider is the RemoteConfigProvider returned by enable_remote_config_api.

docs.title: How it reads
docs.text:
• The request is a JSON body. A plain model parameter on the dependency function (req: VMRequest) is parsed as the request body — you don't have to make the coordinates query parameters. FastAPI validates it (running the coordinate allowlist + hierarchy checks) before the dependency runs.
  • req.metadata drives the lookup. The coordinate submodel is passed to resolve_infra_config, which returns the merged config for that leaf. Your config places each field's allowed values under a known key (os_templates, instance_sizes, …).
  • The constrained fields can sit anywhere in the body — here they're under spec, reached with plain attribute access (req.spec.os_template). Match the loc to the field's real position so the 422 points clients at the right place.
  • It runs after the model's own validators, so by the time the dependency executes the coordinates are already known-valid.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Per-leaf VM OS templates / images.
  • Instance sizes / flavors permitted in a given region or island.
  • Allowed backup targets or networks per environment.
  • Quotas or feature toggles resolved per leaf.

docs.title: Fail-open vs fail-closed
docs.text: The example is permissive: if the config doesn't list the key (or the list is empty), the field is accepted. That mirrors the coordinate validators, which don't reject when their allowlist is empty (pre-poll or upstream missing). To fail closed instead — reject anything not explicitly allowed — drop the allowed and guard and require a non-empty allowed.

docs.title: Enable the Remote Config API
docs.text: enable_remote_config_api wires a thin authenticated proxy to an upstream Config API onto your app. The upstream resolves hierarchical infrastructure config / naming / project-registry from a set of allocation coordinates (space, network, region, island, environment, project); this capability forwards those coordinates over HTTP, caches the result in memory, and keeps your own Swagger dropdowns and request validation in sync with the upstream's live allowlists.

docs.title: Wire it up
docs.text:
from tashtiot_apis_library import general_create_app
from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template import enable_remote_config_api

app = general_create_app()

provider = enable_remote_config_api(
    app,
    base_url="https://config-api.example.com",  # where the upstream lives
    remote_prefix="/api/v1",  # upstream prefix serving /projects, /config, /naming, /coordinates
    coordinate_paths=[
        "/config",
        "/naming",
    ],  # your routes whose coordinate params get enum dropdowns
)

docs.title: Define routes against the provider
docs.text:
The returned RemoteConfigProvider exposes resolve_infra_config, resolve_naming_convention, get_all_projects, get_coordinate_catalog, and get_coordinate_tree (all cached for cache_ttl seconds, default 60):

from fastapi import Depends
from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.config_api import (
    RequiredInfraMetadata,
    CoordinateCatalogResponse,
    CoordinateTreeResponse,
)


@app.get("/config")
async def get_config(meta: RequiredInfraMetadata = Depends()):
    return await provider.resolve_infra_config(meta)


@app.get("/coordinates", response_model=CoordinateCatalogResponse)
async def get_coordinates():
    # Discovery: the valid values per coordinate level plus the project list.
    return await provider.get_coordinate_catalog()


@app.get("/coordinates/tree", response_model=CoordinateTreeResponse)
async def get_coordinates_tree():
    # Same values, shaped as the nested config hierarchy.
    return await provider.get_coordinate_tree()

Each route listed in coordinate_paths gets the live enum dropdowns injected into its coordinate fields whether they arrive as query/path parameters (a Depends() model, as above) or inside a JSON request body (the model as a plain body parameter). For a body model the enums are written onto the referenced component schema, so a model shared by several routes is decorated once. Enum injection matches by field name, so name the field after its coordinate (region, island, …).

get_coordinate_catalog proxies the upstream's /coordinates route and returns a CoordinateCatalogResponse-shaped dict — the sorted set of values for each of space / network / region / island / environment, plus projects. An unseeded upstream yields empty lists (a valid 200, not a 404).

get_coordinate_tree proxies the upstream's /coordinates/tree route and returns a CoordinateTreeResponse-shaped dict — a nested hierarchy (coordinates: space → network → region → island → sorted env list) plus the flat projects list. An unseeded upstream yields {"coordinates": {}, "projects": []}.

docs.title: What it sets up
docs.text:
• A RemoteConfigProvider (returned) for resolving config / naming / projects.
  • A startup seed + background poller (registered on general_create_app's lifespan). The allowlists are fetched once at startup regardless of enable_polling; with polling on they're then refreshed every poll_interval seconds, hot-patching both the Pydantic validators and the OpenAPI enum dropdowns. Pass enable_polling=False for a one-time snapshot (seed only, no refresh).
  • A pydantic.ValidationError → 422 handler so a coordinate outside its allowlist returns the same shape as any other invalid query parameter.
  • Hierarchical validation. Beyond the flat per-level allowlists, the coordinate models also enforce the live coordinate tree (/coordinates/tree): a child must sit under its selected parent — e.g. an island is only valid within the chosen region. This is a submit-time 422, not a Swagger dropdown (OpenAPI can't express dependent enums); expose /coordinates/tree if a frontend needs cascading selects. It's permissive until the tree is populated and for partial (omitted-coordinate) selections.

docs.title: Seeded once, then refreshed
docs.text:
The allowlists and coordinate tree are fetched once at startup even with enable_polling=False, so validation and enum dropdowns work off that snapshot; polling only keeps them fresh afterward. Two caveats:

  • Before that first fetch completes — a brief window at startup — the allowlists are empty, so validation is permissive (accepts any value) and no dropdowns are injected. This is intentional (InfraMetadata doesn't gate on an empty allowlist).
  • If the app isn't built by general_create_app (nothing launches the registered task), the seed never runs automatically. Drive it yourself:
await provider.crawl_and_sync_keys(app)  # populate the allowlists + tree once

docs.title: Matching routes with coordinate_paths
docs.text:
Each coordinate_paths entry is a regex string, matched with re.fullmatch against every route path. A plain path is just a literal regex that matches only itself (so ["/config", "/naming"] works exactly as you'd expect), but you can also match a family of routes with one entry:

coordinate_paths = [r"/api/v\d+/infra/(config|naming)"]  # one entry, many/versioned routes

Because it's a full-path match, use .* for partials (r"/api/v1/infra/.*"); escape regex metacharacters (., +, …) if you need them literal (rare in paths); FastAPI path params like {id} match literally. An invalid regex raises at wire-up.

Enum injection is otherwise name-matched and additive: a matched route that declares only some coordinates gets dropdowns for just those — there's no "all six required" rule and no error, and any non-coordinate parameters are left untouched. The flip side is that mistakes fail quietly: a pattern that matches no route, or a field named differently from its coordinate, simply gets no dropdown (no warning). Name coordinate fields after their coordinate (region, island, …).

docs.title: Serve stale on upstream failure
docs.text:
By default an unreachable or 5xx upstream propagates as a 502 (the strict, fail-closed contract). Pass serve_stale_on_error=True to instead fall back to the last successfully-fetched value for that key (last-known-good) when the upstream is down:

provider = enable_remote_config_api(app, ..., serve_stale_on_error=True)

Notes:

  • Any upstream error except 404 falls back — unreachable host, 5xx, or 4xx (all map to a 502 internally). A 404 is not an error: it means "no value yet" and returns the empty default.
  • The last-known-good store is unbounded (never expires), separate from the cache_ttl cache, so a key that was fetched once stays serveable through an outage of any length.
  • A key never fetched successfully has no fallback, so its first request during an outage still 502s.

docs.title: Choose the outbound auth
docs.text:
Authentication to the upstream is selectable via CONFIG_REMOTE_* environment variables — CONFIG_REMOTE_AUTH_METHOD picks sso (OAuth2 client_credentials), bearer (a static token), or none. See the Remote Config configuration table.

With the default sso method, the config provider mints its token with the same client_credentials machinery as any outbound SSO call. To set it up, ask the SSO team for a client and give its id/secret to CONFIG_REMOTE_SSO_CLIENT_ID / CONFIG_REMOTE_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET. If the upstream Config API checks its audience, also request the optional client scope that carries the platform audience — that scope should already exist in the SSO, so the client just needs it granted — and set CONFIG_REMOTE_SSO_SCOPE to it. (Auth0-style providers can instead send the audience as a parameter via CONFIG_REMOTE_SSO_AUDIENCE.) The same pattern for securing your own API is covered in Secure an API with OIDC & JWKS.

To override settings entirely (tests / escape hatch), pass an explicit httpx.Auth:

from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.security import StaticBearerAuth

provider = enable_remote_config_api(app, ..., auth=StaticBearerAuth("token"))

Lazy dependency

Remote Config pulls in aiocache for its in-memory cache. Because both the cache and enable_remote_config_api import lazily, apps that don't call it never need aiocache.

docs.title: Extend the FastAPI template
docs.text:
general_create_app() returns a plain FastAPI instance, so as a consumer you can add your own routes and middleware to it directly — no library changes needed:

app = general_create_app()


@app.get("/custom")
def custom():
    return {"ok": True}

This guide is for contributors adding a built-in piece to the template — one that ships behind an enable_* flag on the factory. The factory wires each built-in through small registration helpers under _internal/, toggled by a keyword argument.

docs.title: Add a built-in middleware
docs.text:
1. Create it under _internal/middlewares/:
# _internal/middlewares/my_middleware.py
from fastapi import Request
from loguru import logger
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware


class MyMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next):
        logger.debug("before {}", request.url.path)
        response = await call_next(request)
        return response
  1. Register it in add_middlewares (_internal/middlewares/__init__.py) behind a flag:
def add_middlewares(app, *, enable_my_middleware: bool = True, ...):
    if enable_my_middleware:
        app.add_middleware(MyMiddleware)

Mind ordering: Starlette applies middleware LIFO, so auth/logging/timing are registered in a specific order — add yours where it belongs in that chain.

  1. Thread the flag through general_create_app (_internal/__init__.py), passing it into add_middlewares(app, enable_my_middleware=enable_my_middleware, ...).

docs.title: Add a built-in route
docs.text:
1. Create a router under _internal/routes/:
# _internal/routes/my_route.py
from fastapi import APIRouter

router = APIRouter(prefix="/my-feature", tags=["My Feature"])


@router.get("/status")
async def status():
    return {"status": "ok"}
  1. Register it in add_routers (_internal/routes/__init__.py) behind a flag:
def add_routers(app, *, enable_my_route: bool = True, ...):
    if enable_my_route:
        app.include_router(router)   # add include_in_schema=False to hide from /docs
  1. Thread an enable_my_route flag through general_create_app.

docs.title: Add a shared utility
docs.text: Put reusable internals under _internal/utils/ (or _internal/database/ for HTTP). To make a utility public, re-export it from the matching public module — fastapi_template/utils.py (infra), auth.py (inbound JWT), security.py (outbound SSO), or errors.py — and add it to that module's __all__. Keep heavy dependencies lazy where the existing modules do (see Architecture).

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• New code uses relative imports and logs via from loguru import logger at the standard levels.
  • Every built-in is opt-out-able via an enable_* flag (default chosen sensibly).
  • Public symbols land on the narrow public surface; implementation stays under _internal/.
  • Tests added under tests/fastapi_template/.

docs.title: Generate dev auth material
docs.text: The package installs a gen-auth-material console script that mints an RSA keypair and a signed JWT for exercising local public-key inbound auth. It's the signing-side companion to the verifier — handy for local development and tests, where you don't want to stand up a real identity provider.

docs.title: Common recipes
docs.text:
# Write jwt_private.pem + jwt_public.pem, print a non-expiring token
gen-auth-material

# Mint a token that expires in 30 minutes instead
gen-auth-material --expires-minutes 30

# Print a keypair + token, write nothing to disk
gen-auth-material --no-write

# Set claims to match the verifier's AUTH_AUDIENCE / AUTH_ISSUER
gen-auth-material --sub svc --aud my-api --iss https://idp/

# Reuse existing keys, mint a fresh token
gen-auth-material --private-key jwt_private.pem

You can also run it as a module: python -m tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template._internal.security.keygen.

docs.title: Using the output
docs.text:
Point a verifying service at the generated public key:

AUTH_ENABLED=true
AUTH_PUBLIC_KEY_PATH=jwt_public.pem
AUTH_REQUIRE_EXP=false        # only needed for the default non-expiring token

Then send the printed token as Authorization: Bearer <token>. The Secure your API tutorial walks through this end-to-end.

Non-expiring by default

Without --expires-minutes, the minted token has no exp claim and never expires. The verifier requires exp out of the box, so the verifying service must set AUTH_REQUIRE_EXP=false to accept it (the CLI prints this hint).

docs.title: Migrate an API to the current library version
docs.text:
Use this prompt with an AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, …), run inside the API's repository, to move the API onto the current tashtiot-apis-library release and the API standards.

The prompt first picks one of two modes:

Mode When Result A: Upgrade The API already uses the library, on an older version The smallest safe change. Applies the version-specific upgrade notes and non-breaking fixes. The public contract is kept, and breaking deviations are only reported. B: Rewrite The API doesn't use the library, or you want a full rewrite The API is rebuilt on the library to the full standards ({metadata, spec}, connectors, async, auth, Remote Config if needed). It ships as a new major version.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Copy the prompt below (use the copy button), or take it from prompts/migrate-api.md in the library repository.
  2. Run it in the API's repository, on a new branch. Review the agent's mode choice and its "Needs a decision" list before merging.

Note

The prompt is updated with every library release, so always take the latest copy. The target version is stated at the top of the prompt.

docs.text:
<pre><code><!--
  MAINTAINERS: keep this prompt in step with the library.
  On EVERY release, update:
    1. TARGET_VERSION below, the version in the dependency line in step A1, and the git tag in
       every apis-library source link (/tree/vX.Y.Z/),
    2. the "Upgrade notes by version" table (add a row for anything a consumer must change or verify),
