# Migrate an API to tashtiot-apis-library 1.3.2

TARGET_VERSION: **1.3.2**

You are migrating the API in the current repository to **`tashtiot-apis-library` 1.3.2** and to the
company **API standards**. You are working as a careful senior engineer: you read the code before
changing it, you verify every library name against the library's source, and you never guess.

## Sources of truth (read these, don't rely on memory)

1. **The library source at the target tag:**
   <https://github.com/Platform-Infra-Org/apis-library/tree/v1.3.2/src/tashtiot_apis_library>.
   Every import, class, method and argument you use must exist there. If the docs and the source
   disagree, the source wins. Read it from GitHub, or from a local clone checked out at `v1.3.2`.

   **Don't rely on an installed copy.** The package is private. It can only be `pip`/`uv` installed
   from Artifactory **inside the air-gapped network**, so outside it there is no installed copy to
   read. Don't switch the dependency to a git URL to work around this.

2. **The library docs**, <https://platform-infra-org.github.io/apis-library/>, especially:
    - [API standards](https://platform-infra-org.github.io/apis-library/reference/api-standards/): the rules this migration must meet.
    - [Async and the event loop](https://platform-infra-org.github.io/apis-library/explanation/async/),
      [Job queues & long-running work](https://platform-infra-org.github.io/apis-library/explanation/job-queues/) and
      [Cloud-native APIs & multiple replicas](https://platform-infra-org.github.io/apis-library/explanation/cloud-native/).
    - [How-to guides](https://platform-infra-org.github.io/apis-library/how-to/) for connectors, OIDC/JWKS, outbound SSO and the Remote Config
      API.
    - [Changelog](https://platform-infra-org.github.io/apis-library/changelog/): every change between the API's current version and 1.3.2.
3. **The `example-api` repository**, <https://github.com/Platform-Infra-Org/example-api>: the reference implementation of the structure.
   Follow its layout, but not the items listed under
   [Known gaps in `example-api`](https://platform-infra-org.github.io/apis-library/reference/api-standards/#known-gaps-in-example-api).

## Step 0: Choose the migration mode

Inspect the repository, then pick **exactly one** mode, and state which one and why before you change
anything:

| | **Mode A: Upgrade** | **Mode B: Rewrite** |
|---|---|---|
| **When** | The API already depends on `tashtiot-apis-library` (any version: check `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, `requirements*.txt`, `setup.py`) | The API does **not** use the library (plain FastAPI, Flask, another framework, its own HTTP clients, sync code), **or** the user explicitly asks for a full rewrite |
| **Goal** | Move to 1.3.2 with the **smallest safe change** | Rebuild the API on the library so it fully meets the API standards |
| **Public contract** (paths, request/response shapes, status codes) | **Preserved.** Anything in the standards that would break callers is *reported*, not changed | **Redesigned to the standards** (`{metadata, spec}`, 202 for async work, …). It's a breaking change, so it ships as a **new major version** of the API |
| **Scope** | Dependency bump, the version-specific changes below, non-breaking conformance fixes | Everything: layout, config, connectors, async, auth, Remote Config, errors, tests, Docker, CI, changelog |

If the repository matches neither, or the user's intent is unclear, **stop and ask** which mode
they want.

## Ground rules (both modes)

- Work on a new branch. Run the existing test suite **before** you change anything and record the
  result, so you can tell pre-existing failures from new ones.
- Make the change in small, reviewable steps. Keep the app booting and the tests passing after each
  one.
- **Never block the event loop:** no `requests`, `time.sleep`, `subprocess.run` or sync DB/SDK
  clients inside `async def` code. Use the library's async connectors, `BaseAPI`,
  `asyncio.sleep`, `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec` or `asyncio.to_thread`.
- **Never import from `tashtiot_apis_library...._internal`.** Use only the public modules in the quick
  reference below.
- **Secrets** never go into code, `conf.py` defaults, `.env.example`, logs, tests or the image. Use
  placeholders in `.env.example`.
- **Authorization is handled outside the APIs.** Inbound auth only verifies the JWT (signature, expiry,
  audience). Don't add permission checks on token claims. If the existing code has some, don't port
  them, and list them in the report so the team can confirm they are enforced elsewhere.
- Don't add dependencies for things the library, FastAPI or the standard library already provide.
- When a decision belongs to the team (changing a public contract, removing a route, dropping
  existing authorization logic, choosing a job-queue solution), **ask**. Don't decide alone.

---

## Mode A: Upgrade from an earlier library version

### A1. Bump the dependency

- Set `tashtiot-apis-library>=1.3.2` in `pyproject.toml`. If the API still uses `setup.py` or
  `requirements.txt`, move it to `pyproject.toml` + **uv** (`uv.lock` committed, `uv.toml` never
  committed).
- Python must be **>= 3.10** (the company standard is 3.12: `.python-version`,
  `requires-python`, Dockerfile base image).
- Remove any local path override of the library (`[tool.uv.sources]`) unless the user says it is
  intentional for local development.
- **Inside the air-gapped network:** run `uv lock && uv sync --group dev`.
- **Outside it:** Artifactory isn't reachable, so `uv lock` / `uv sync` can't resolve the library.
  Leave the dependency line as `tashtiot-apis-library>=1.3.2`. Don't commit a stale or hand-edited
  `uv.lock`, and say in the report that the lock must be regenerated inside the network.

### A2. Apply the upgrade notes for every version you cross

Find the API's current library version, then apply **every row newer than it**, top to bottom.

| If the API is on… | Change or verify |
|---|---|
| **< 1.0.0** (0.x) | **Background tasks now actually run.** In 0.x, `general_create_app(async_background_tasks=[...])` accepted the list but never started it. From 1.0.0 every coroutine in it is launched at startup and cancelled on shutdown. Check that each one is safe to run, and remove any workaround that starts them another way (`@app.on_event("startup")`, a manual `create_task`), or they will run twice. |
| | **Don't pass your own `lifespan=`** to `general_create_app`. The library sets one, and a second raises `TypeError`. Register startup work through `async_background_tasks` (or append to `app.state.async_background_tasks` before startup). |
| | **Removed:** `tashtiot_apis_library.terraform_runner` and `fastapi_template._internal.models` (`ExceptionHandlerConfig`). Replace any usage. Never import `_internal`. |
| | **Inbound auth is available:** call `general_create_app(enable_auth=True, ...)`. It changes nothing until `AUTH_ENABLED=true` is set. Configure it per *Authentication* below. If the API had its own JWT check, replace it with the library's middleware and `get_current_claims`. |
| | **New request bases:** `InfraOperationRequest` / `RequiredInfraOperationRequest` (live-validated coordinates). The old `OperationRequest` requires `project`, `network`, `region`, `space` and `environment`, but the standard requires **only `project`**. Moving to the `ProjectMetadata` pattern (below) makes four fields optional, which is a non-breaking relaxation, so do it. |
| | **Outbound SSO and Remote Config** are now available (`fastapi_template.security`, `enable_remote_config_api`). Adopt them only where the API needs them (see below). |
| **< 1.1.0** | `enable_remote_config_api(..., serve_stale_on_error=...)` is new (default `False`, so behaviour is unchanged). Expose it as a setting if the team wants last-known-good config during upstream outages. |
| **< 1.1.2** | **`enable_remote_config_api` signature changed:** `config_path=` and `naming_path=` were replaced by **`coordinate_paths=[...]`**, a list of **regex strings** matched with `re.fullmatch` against route paths. Rewrite the call. The coordinate allowlists are now seeded once at startup even with `enable_polling=False`, and enums are injected into nested request-body models too. |
| **< 1.2.0** | `ArgoCD.create_app` / `ArgoCD.delete_app` are new. Replace any hand-rolled ArgoCD Application create/delete calls with them. |
| **< 1.2.1** | `Git(..., ssh_port=7995)` is now configurable (default unchanged). If the API patched the port, remove the patch and pass `ssh_port`. |
| **< 1.2.3** | **AWX status codes changed.** `AWX.get_job_status` / `get_workflow_job_status` used to return `status_code=200` for every state. They now map the AWX state: `pending`/`waiting`/`running` → **202**, `successful` → 200, `failed`/`error`/`canceled` → **500**. Launch calls still return `status="successful"`, `status_code=200`. Find every place that reads `status_code` from an AWX status response (route return values, `JSONResponse(status_code=...)`, tests, clients) and confirm the new values are intended. |
| **< 1.3.0** | `AWX.get_job_output(job_id, start_line=..., page_size=...)` (incremental playbook output) is new. Adopt it only if the API streams or polls job output. |
| **< 1.3.1** | `AWX.get_job_status` / `get_workflow_job_status` take a new keyword-only `include_logs=False`. With `True`, `stdout` carries a concise, filtered log summary (child jobs and failed-job output for workflows). The default is unchanged. Adopt it if the API's status route should return readable logs. |
| **< 1.3.2** | **Validation errors no longer expose submitted values.** 422 response bodies now contain only `loc`, `msg` and `type` for each error, with no `input` or `ctx`. The validation log line is now `Validation error on <METHOD> <path>: [...]`, without the values or a traceback. Update any test or client that reads `input`/`ctx` from a 422 or asserts on the old log text. Make sure the API's own validator messages don't include the submitted value, because the library can't strip those. |

### A3. Non-breaking conformance fixes

Bring the code in line with the API standards **wherever it doesn't change the public contract**:

- Connectors built once in `create_app()` and injected through router factories, never per request.
- Blocking calls replaced with async equivalents. `BaseAPI` used with `async with`, and TLS
  verification turned on where the service has a valid certificate.
- `ExternalServiceError` caught in routes and mapped to 502. Error `detail` has no secrets.
- Background tasks kept referenced (a module-level `set` + `add_done_callback(discard)`) and logging
  their own exceptions.
- Settings the library owns (`AUTH_*`, `AUTH_SSO_*`, `CONFIG_REMOTE_*`, `PORT`, `LOG_LEVEL`,
  `PROXIED`, …) removed from the API's own `BaseSettings`. `.env.example` lists every variable.
- Loguru with `{}` placeholders, no `print`, no secrets in logs.
- Tests: hermetic env, valid bearer for route tests, connectors mocked, no real network calls.

### A4. Report what you didn't change

List every remaining deviation from the standards that **would** break callers (for example: a write
route without `metadata`, `200`/`201` returned for work that is still running, a non-standard path
or version prefix). For each one, propose the fix and say it needs a new API version. Don't apply
these unless the user approves.

---

## Mode B: Rewrite onto the library and the API standards

### B1. Inventory the existing API (before writing code)

Produce a table, and show it to the user, covering:

- Every endpoint: method, path, request and response shape, status codes, whether it is
  long-running.
- Every external system it calls (AWX, ArgoCD, Bitbucket, Vault, others), and how (library, own
  client, sync/async).
- Auth today (inbound and outbound), and any authorization logic.
- Configuration and secrets (env vars, files).
- Background or periodic work.
- Tests, Dockerfile and CI that exist.

Then confirm with the user: the new API name and path prefix (`/api/<api-name>/v<N>/...`), the new
major version, and whether the old version must keep running alongside it during the transition.

### B2. Scaffold the standard layout

Follow the "Project layout" in the API standards (`app/main.py`, `app/global_conf.py`,
`app/schemas.py`, and `app/v<N>/<resource>/{conf,schemas,operations,routes}.py`), with
`general_create_app(enable_auth=True, title=..., version=APP_VERSION)` as the single wiring point.

### B3. Request and response contract

- Every write route takes `{"metadata": {...}, "spec": {...}}`, with `metadata` typed as
  `ProjectMetadata` (below): `project` required, the other coordinates optional. Metadata the API
  doesn't use is accepted and ignored.
- `spec` holds the resource's desired state, with typed, validated fields.
- Responses use `response_model=` and extend `OperationResponse` / `AWXOperationResponse` /
  `ArgoOperationResponse`.
- Status codes follow the standards table: **202 + an id** for work that finishes asynchronously, and
  **502** for upstream failures.

### B4. Connectors and async

- Replace each external call with the library connector (`AWX`, `ArgoCD`, `Git` for Bitbucket
  Server, `Vault`). Use `BaseAPI` for any other HTTP service, or `sso_authenticated_api` when the
  service needs an SSO token.
- Convert the code path to `async def` end to end. Every network call is awaited and has a timeout.
  Run independent calls with `asyncio.gather`.
- Multi-step operations (for example Git → Vault → ArgoCD): snapshot before changing, compensate in
  reverse order on failure, log failed compensations, and make every step idempotent.
- If a connector is missing something more than one team would need, note it as a library
  contribution instead of building a private client.

### B5. Long-running work

- Work that runs as an **AWX job** returns 202 with the AWX `job_id`, plus a
  `GET .../status/{job_id}` route that calls `awx.get_job_status`. AWX is the job queue.
- Short, best-effort follow-ups may use a referenced in-process task, with status derived from the
  external system.
- Long work that runs inside the API and must survive restarts needs a job queue. **The library has
  none.** Stop and ask the team whether to implement one, use an external solution, or move the work
  into AWX.

### B6. Authentication and Remote Config

Configure them per the sections below.

### B7. Errors, logging, tests, packaging, CI

- Map `ExternalServiceError` to 502. Use Loguru, with no secrets in logs.
- Tests: schemas (valid, invalid, project-only metadata, extra metadata keys), routes through
  `TestClient(create_app())` with an HS256 bearer, auth (401/401/200), operation failure and
  rollback paths, and Remote Config fallback. No real network calls.
- `pyproject.toml` + uv, `.env.example`, `README.md`.
- A Dockerfile following `example-api`'s, with the base image from JFrog Artifactory.
- `.woodpecker/` pipeline per the CI how-to in the internal Confluence: tests, formatting, linting, SonarQube, then build and
  push to JFrog Artifactory.
- `cliff.toml` (copy `example-api`'s) and a `CHANGELOG.md` generated by git-cliff. PR titles are
  conventional commits.

---

## Authentication (both modes)

- **Inbound:** `general_create_app(enable_auth=True)`. Enforced only when `AUTH_ENABLED=true`, with
  exactly **one** verification mode set:
    - Production: `AUTH_OIDC_ISSUER` or `AUTH_JWKS_URL`, plus **`AUTH_AUDIENCE`**.
    - Offline: `AUTH_PUBLIC_KEY_PEM` / `AUTH_PUBLIC_KEY_PATH`.
    - Tests and local dev: `AUTH_HS256_SECRET`.

  Read claims with `Depends(get_current_claims)`. Probes, `/metrics` and `/docs` stay excluded.
  Add the variables, commented, to `.env.example`.
- **Outbound** (only if the API calls protected services): `sso_authenticated_api(base_url)`, configured
  by `AUTH_SSO_TOKEN_URL`, `AUTH_SSO_CLIENT_ID`, `AUTH_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET` (+ optional `AUTH_SSO_SCOPE`,
  `AUTH_SSO_AUDIENCE`). Catch `AuthConfigError` and return a clean error. Don't cache tokens
  yourself.
- **No authorization logic in the API** (see Ground rules).

## Remote Config provider (only if needed)

Use it **only** if some value varies by environment or coordinate (AWX template ids, endpoints,
quotas…). If nothing does, skip it, and say so in the report.

- Wire it **opt-in**: only when `CONFIG_API_URL` is set, wrapped in
  `try/except AuthConfigError`, and passing `coordinate_paths=[...]` (regex strings for the routes
  whose metadata should get live dropdowns).
- In operations: `resolved = await provider.resolve_infra_config(payload.metadata)`, then
  `resolved.get("<key>", config.<STATIC_DEFAULT>)`. There is always a static fallback.
- Upstream auth comes from `CONFIG_REMOTE_AUTH_METHOD` (`sso` / `bearer` / `none`) and the matching
  `CONFIG_REMOTE_*` variables.

## The `ProjectMetadata` pattern

```python
# app/schemas.py
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.config_api import InfraMetadata


class ProjectMetadata(InfraMetadata):
    """Platform metadata: project required, every other coordinate optional."""

    project: str = Field(..., description="The platform application submitting the request")


class MetadataRequest(BaseModel):
    metadata: ProjectMetadata = Field(..., description="Platform metadata (project required).")


# app/v1/<resource>/schemas.py
class CreateThing(MetadataRequest):
    spec: CreateThingSpec
```

docs.title: Read & write Bitbucket files
docs.text: Use the Git connector to manipulate files in a Bitbucket Server repository over its HTTP API (with SSH used for delete operations). All methods are async.

docs.title: Construct the client
docs.text:
from tashtiot_apis_library import Git

git = Git(
    base_url="https://bitbucket.example.com",  # base Bitbucket URL
    token="token",  # HTTP token with write access
    username_or_email="user@example.com",  # service account identity
    project_key="PROJ",  # Bitbucket project key
    repo_slug="repo-name",  # repo name, lowercase
    default_ref="main",  # default branch to operate on
    ssh_key_file_path="/path/to/ssh/private/key",  # SSH key (used for delete)
)

docs.title: Read a file
docs.text:
content = await git.get_file_content("/path/to/values.yaml")  # returns str

Parse it however you like — for example, as YAML:

import yaml

data = yaml.safe_load(await git.get_file_content("/app/values.yaml"))

docs.title: Add, modify, and delete files
docs.text:
await git.add_file("/new/file.txt", "Add file", "hello world")
await git.modify_file("/app/values.yaml", "Bump replicas", new_yaml_str)
await git.delete_file("/old/file.txt", "Remove obsolete file")

Each takes a commit message; pass branch= to target a branch other than default_ref.

entries = await git.list_dir("/app")  # List[Tuple[name, type]]
all_files = await git.list_files_recursive("/app")  # List[str]
exists = await git.file_exists("/app/values.yaml")  # bool

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
import asyncio
import yaml
from tashtiot_apis_library import Git


async def main():
    git = Git(
        base_url="https://bitbucket.example.com",
        token="token",
        username_or_email="user@example.com",
        project_key="PROJ",
        repo_slug="repo-name",
        default_ref="main",
        ssh_key_file_path="/path/to/ssh/private/key",
    )
    values = yaml.safe_load(await git.get_file_content("/app/values.yaml"))
    print(values)


asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Secure an API with OIDC & JWKS
docs.text:
To protect your service against tokens minted by the platform SSO, verify inbound bearer tokens in JWKS mode: the verifier fetches the provider's RS256 signing keys from its JWKS endpoint (by their kid) and validates every request against them. This is the standards path for any OIDC provider and needs no shared secret or key file on your side — unlike the local-pubkey mode used in the Secure your API tutorial.

Two sides have to line up: the SSO (issues tokens carrying the right audience), and your API (verifies the signature, iss, and aud). Callers get their tokens via the OAuth2 client_credentials grant.

docs.title: 1. What to request from the SSO team
docs.text:
The verification material and the audience aren't something you generate — ask the SSO team for:

  • A client (client id + secret) for each caller that will reach your API. Callers use it with the client_credentials grant (see step 3). Human callers front-ended by a UI use their own flow; this is for service-to-service calls.
  • An audience (a.k.a. API identifier) for your service — the value the SSO stamps into the aud claim of issued tokens, and the value your API checks. Agree on one string (e.g. https://my-api.platform.example).
  • The client scope that carries the platform audience. On Keycloak-style providers the aud is set by an Audience protocol mapper attached to a client scope. This platform scope should already exist in the SSO — callers just need it granted/requested so their tokens carry your audience. (On Auth0-style providers the audience is a request parameter instead — see step 3.)
  • The issuer URL (for OIDC discovery) or the JWKS endpoint URL directly.

docs.title: 2. Configure your API (inbound verification)
docs.text:
Turn on inbound auth. It's dual-gated — both the code flag and the runtime switch must be set:

from tashtiot_apis_library import general_create_app

app = general_create_app(enable_auth=True)  # gate 1: the code flag

Point the verifier at the SSO in your environment (.env or process env). Prefer OIDC discovery — give it the issuer and it fetches /.well-known/openid-configuration at startup to find the jwks_uri:

AUTH_ENABLED=true                                        # gate 2: the runtime switch
AUTH_OIDC_ISSUER=https://sso.platform.example/realms/platform
AUTH_AUDIENCE=https://my-api.platform.example            # must equal the audience the SSO assigned you

Or skip discovery and name the JWKS endpoint directly (use one or the other, not both):

AUTH_ENABLED=true
AUTH_JWKS_URL=https://sso.platform.example/realms/platform/protocol/openid-connect/certs
AUTH_AUDIENCE=https://my-api.platform.example
AUTH_ISSUER=https://sso.platform.example/realms/platform  # expected iss (OIDC discovery sets this for you)

Set AUTH_AUDIENCE or audience isn't checked

Audience is validated only when AUTH_AUDIENCE is set. Leave it unset and any validly-signed token from the issuer is accepted regardless of who it was minted for — so a token meant for a different service would pass. Always set it to your assigned audience.

With enable_auth=True + AUTH_ENABLED=true, the AuthMiddleware protects every route (minus the exclude list: probes, docs, /.well-known, …). Routes read the verified identity via Depends(get_current_claims); a missing or invalid token gets a 401. See the full inbound AUTH_* table for every knob (AUTH_ISSUER, AUTH_ALGORITHMS, AUTH_JWKS_CACHE_TTL, AUTH_REQUIRE_EXP, …).

docs.title: 3. How a caller obtains a token (client_credentials)
docs.text:
A caller exchanges its client id/secret for a token at the SSO's token endpoint, then sends it as Authorization: Bearer <token>. The issued token's aud must match your AUTH_AUDIENCE, so the caller has to make the SSO stamp it:

  • Keycloak-style: request the platform client scope (step 1) so the Audience mapper adds your aud. With this library's helpers, set AUTH_SSO_SCOPE to that scope.
  • Auth0-style: the provider honours an audience request parameter — set AUTH_SSO_AUDIENCE to your audience and the IdP stamps it.

If the caller is itself a service built on this library, it doesn't need to hand-roll the grant — the outbound helpers fetch, cache, and refresh the token automatically:

from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.security import sso_authenticated_api

async with sso_authenticated_api("https://my-api.platform.example") as client:
    resp = await client.get("/protected")  # Authorization: Bearer <auto-managed>

See Call other services with SSO for the full outbound setup (AUTH_SSO_* variables, per-upstream SSOConfig, and how the downstream aud is populated).

docs.title: Drive AWX, ArgoCD & Vault
docs.text: Recipes for the remaining three connectors. All methods are async; construct each client with its base URL and a token.

docs.title: AWX — launch a job and await it
docs.text:
from tashtiot_apis_library import AWX

awx = AWX(base_url="https://awx.example.com", token="token")

# Launch a job template; returns an AWXOperationResponse (carries job_id)
response = await awx.launch_job(job_template_id=1, extra_vars={"env": "prod"})

# Block until it finishes, then inspect the standardized result
result = await awx.wait_for_job_completion(response.job_id)
if result.status == "successful":
    print(f"Job {result.job_id} finished!")

launch_workflow_job / wait_for_workflow_completion do the same for workflow job templates, and get_job_status(job_id) polls a single status.

Standardized responses

Service methods return OperationResponse subclasses, not raw API payloads. The base carries status, status_code, return_code, and stdout; AWXOperationResponse adds job_id and ArgoOperationResponse adds app_name. See the Schemas reference.

docs.title: ArgoCD — sync an app and wait for it
docs.text:
from tashtiot_apis_library import ArgoCD

argo = ArgoCD(
    base_url="https://argo.example.com",
    api_key="token",
    application_set_timeout=30,  # seconds to wait for sync/delete
)

await argo.sync("my-app")
app = await argo.wait_for_update("my-app")  # ArgoApplication once healthy/synced
status = await argo.get_app_status("my-app")  # ArgoOperationResponse

Other helpers include wait_for_app_creation, wait_for_app_deletion, get_app_values, modify_values, get_app_parameters, and modify_parameters.

docs.title: Vault — read and write secrets
docs.text:
from tashtiot_apis_library import Vault

vault = Vault(base_url="https://vault.example.com", token="token")

secret = await vault.read_secret("secret/data/myapp")  # VaultSecret (.data, .metadata)
await vault.write_secret("secret/data/myapp", {"api_key": "value"})
await vault.delete_secret("secret/data/myapp")

write_secret accepts a plain mapping, a VaultSecretPayload, or any Pydantic model (it is dumped to a dict, dropping Nones).

docs.title: Incremental AWX playbook output for an Argo dispatcher
docs.text:
get_job_output is an opt-in method for single playbook jobs, including jobs launched by the CloudCore/Linux APIs. An Argo Workflow and an AWX workflow job are different: this method does not aggregate child jobs of an AWX workflow job.

chunk = await awx.get_job_output(job_id, start_line=0, page_size=100)
# Serialize chunk with model_dump(mode="json") in your API.
# On the dispatcher: print chunk.stdout, then retain chunk.next_line per job.

The response includes existing status, status_code, job_id, stdout fields plus:

  • next_line: the next AWX stdout position; send it as start_line on the next request.
  • has_more: another page or a gap in arriving events requires another fetch.
  • finished: the job is terminal, AWX reports event_processing_finished=true, and this chunk drains the available output. Print this chunk before stopping.

An API may expose a separate output endpoint returning HTTP 200 for successful reads, with job status in the JSON. The status_code field remains the existing AWX status mapping; it is not the transport status of this separate output endpoint. Keep the existing status endpoint unchanged. The dispatcher must stop on finished, not merely a successful job status, and determine its final exit code from status. Failed/canceled jobs can still have output to drain. Network/auth errors are request failures; do not advance the cursor on them. Retain a total wait timeout, including while waiting for late output or missing processing metadata.

The implementation reads one page from /api/v2/jobs/{id}/job_events/, ordered by stdout position, and advances only through contiguous lines. Empty reads leave the cursor unchanged. Drain pages immediately while has_more is true and next_line advances. If the cursor does not advance (a gap), sleep before retrying to avoid a busy loop. Zero-line events are filtered before pagination so they cannot block the cursor. Page size bounds the number of events, not their byte size. AWX output is returned explicitly; the library does not automatically log playbook output or expose event_data/variables. Output can itself contain sensitive playbook values, so use the same access restrictions as the existing job and AWX's no_log protections. Cursors are job-specific; persist them outside the process if the dispatcher must resume after a restart. This is not exactly-once delivery across crashes.

The API must authorize access to each job, just as the status endpoint does. No AWX token is passed to the dispatcher. A FastAPI response model must preserve the new fields rather than downcast to AWXOperationResponse.

docs.title: Local check without AWX or Tyk
docs.text:
DEBUG=false .venv/bin/pytest tests/connectors/test_awx_output.py tests/connectors/test_awx_client.py --no-cov
DEBUG=false PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python examples/awx_output_demo.py

The demo uses mocked AWX HTTP responses and an in-process FastAPI endpoint, then prints three incremental chunks from a dispatcher-like HTTP client. The simulated playbook adds these chunks while the dispatcher sleeps; the dispatcher then drains multiple pages without sleeping again. The GitHub checks workflow also runs this simulation. It needs the dev dependencies. This validates the library and proposed HTTP contract, not the closed-network API or Tyk. Before promotion, verify the deployed AWX exposes start_line, end_line, event_processing_finished, supports the event filters, and permits the API token to read job events. Older versions lacking completion metadata will time out rather than silently claim all output was delivered.

The event ordering/completion approach follows the AWX CLI monitor.

docs.title: Concise status summaries (jobs and workflow jobs)
docs.text:
For the Linux API/Dispatcher integration that already prints response bodies, use include_logs=True on the existing status methods:

# Inside your existing JOBSTATUS handler; return the result as before.
result = await awx.get_workflow_job_status(workflow_job_id, include_logs=True)
# Or, for a standalone playbook job:
result = await awx.get_job_status(job_id, include_logs=True)

Both still return AWXOperationResponse, with the same status and HTTP-code mapping. The optional summary fills stdout; the default (False) preserves existing behavior. Keep your API's existing authentication and response-code handling. There is no need for a new endpoint or cursor in the dispatcher for this snapshot mode. The dispatcher must display the response's stdout (its existing response-body logging may show it as JSON with escaped newlines; printing stdout separately gives readable lines).

Example workflow stdout:

[✓] Create VM: successful
[✓] Configure Linux: successful
[✗] Install monitoring: failed
  TASK [Install monitoring agent]
  fatal: [server-01]: FAILED!
    → No package monitoring-agent available
  PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
  server-01 : ok=4 changed=2 unreachable=0 failed=1 skipped=0 rescued=0 ignored=0

Workflow summaries list started child jobs and fetch the last ten filtered lines only for failed, errored, or canceled playbook jobs. Project-update nodes are skipped. Nested workflow jobs are traversed, with cycle/depth protection. Other node types show status only; nodes without a job or job summary are omitted. Node pages are read in ID order (not a chronological merge of parallel output), up to 100 pages of 100 nodes. Standalone jobs show their heading plus the last two recap lines on success, or ten filtered lines on failure/error/cancellation. Pending/running states use a neutral icon.

The filter retains play/task headers, action results, warnings, errors, short messages, and play recap. It strips ANSI colors and omits verbose module result bodies. It keeps at most 100 selected lines and 10,000 characters per filtered log and caps the combined workflow summary at 10,000 characters with a truncation marker. These are output limits; AWX's plain-text stdout response is still fetched in full. This is a presentation filter, not secret redaction: task names and messages may still include sensitive data.

This is a snapshot summary, not incremental streaming: repeated polls may repeat headings/output, successful workflow children do not include their full playbook output, and the existing status completion does not wait for late AWX event processing. Use get_job_output when incremental, fully drained single-job output is required. Optional log/node retrieval errors produce an unavailable marker and a warning while preserving the primary status. Errors fetching the primary status still raise normally.

Preview locally without AWX/Tyk:

DEBUG=false PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python examples/awx_status_summary_demo.py

AWX exposes workflow nodes and job stdout through its API. The API's AWX token must have permission to read those resources.

docs.title: Verify a token outside a request
docs.text:
The auth middleware verifies tokens for inbound HTTP requests automatically. When you need to verify a token outside the request flow — in a background worker, a CLI, or a route that receives the token by other means — use the standalone verify_token helper.

from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.auth import verify_token
from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.errors import TokenError

try:
    claims = verify_token(token)  # returns the decoded claims dict
except TokenError as exc:
    ...  # invalid signature, expired, wrong audience, etc.

verify_token uses the same configuration as the middleware (it reads the package settings), so it honours whatever verification material and claim checks you've configured via AUTH_* environment variables — see Configuration.

docs.title: Verify against a different configuration
docs.text:
Pass an explicit settings object to verify against a configuration other than the package default — useful when one worker validates tokens from several issuers:

claims = verify_token(token, settings=other_settings)

docs.title: Server-side verification of SSO-issued tokens
docs.text:
To verify tokens minted by an SSO provider (the outbound side issuing tokens that this service receives), use JWKS mode: point AUTH_JWKS_URL at the provider's JWKS endpoint and set AUTH_AUDIENCE / AUTH_ISSUER to match the issued tokens. Then either protect routes with the middleware (enable_auth=True) or check a token directly with verify_token.

Non-expiring tokens

The verifier requires an exp claim by default. To accept a token minted without one (e.g. a dev token from gen-auth-material), set AUTH_REQUIRE_EXP=false on the verifying service. A token that does carry exp is still validated, so expired tokens remain rejected.

docs.text:
<your-api>/
├── app/
│   ├── main.py            # create_app(): the ONLY wiring point (connectors + routers)
│   ├── global_conf.py     # app-wide BaseSettings -> `global_config`
│   ├── schemas.py         # shared models (e.g. ProjectMetadata)
│   ├── helpers.py         # shared pure helpers (naming conventions, payload parsing)
│   └── v1/

│           ├── conf.py        # module BaseSettings -> `config` (API_PREFIX, API_TAGS, ids…)
│           ├── schemas.py     # Pydantic request/response models ({metadata, spec})
│           ├── operations.py  # business logic; receives connectors as arguments
│           └── routes.py      # get_<resource>_router(deps) -> APIRouter
├── tests/
│   ├── conftest.py        # hermetic env (shadows a developer .env)
│   └── v1/<resource>/     # conftest.py + test_*.py per module
├── .env.example           # every variable, documented. Committed.
├── .env                   # local values. NEVER committed.

├── Dockerfile
├── .woodpecker/build.yaml
└── README.md
Layer May May not routes.py Declare paths, models and status codes; translate exceptions into HTTP responses Contain business logic; construct connectors operations.py Orchestrate connectors; apply business rules; roll back Import Request/Response; read env vars directly schemas.py Define shape and validation Perform I/O conf.py Declare settings with defaults and descriptions Hold real secrets as defaults

docs.title: Application factory
docs.text:
general_create_app() (API reference) provides these built-ins:

Built-in Path / behaviour Flag (default) Request logging middleware Logs every request and response (health/docs/metrics at DEBUG) enable_logging_middleware=True Timing middleware Adds the X-Process-Time header (ns) enable_time_recording_middleware=True Exception handlers HTTPException → {"detail": ...}; validation → 422; anything else → 500 "Internal Server Error" enable_exception_handlers=True Prometheus metrics GET /metrics (+ app_uptime_seconds gauge) enable_metrics_route=True Swagger / ReDoc GET /docs, GET /redoc (self-hosted assets) enable_swagger_routes=True Probes GET /liveness, GET /readiness enable_probe_routes=True Root route GET / → welcome message enable_root_route=True Inbound JWT auth Global middleware (Authentication) enable_auth=False Background tasks Coroutines launched at startup and cancelled on shutdown async_background_tasks=[...]

Any other keyword (title, version, description…) is passed through to FastAPI().

Rules:

  • create_app() in app/main.py is the single wiring point. It builds every connector once, builds Remote Config if needed, and mounts every router.
  • Always pass enable_auth=True. The runtime switch AUTH_ENABLED decides whether auth is enforced.
  • Set title and version (APP_VERSION, injected from the git tag at build time).
  • Something every API needs (a middleware, a route, a utility) goes into the library, not into one API (Extend the FastAPI template).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• All configuration is pydantic-settings BaseSettings, read from environment variables with .env as a fallback. Environment variables take precedence.
  • app/global_conf.py holds settings shared across modules (connector URLs and tokens, TEAM_NAME, CONFIG_API_*, API_TITLE, APP_VERSION) in the singleton global_config.
  • app/v1/<resource>/conf.py holds one module's settings, including API_PREFIX and API_TAGS, in the singleton config.
  • Every field has a description=. Use SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", extra="ignore").
  • Required settings have no default, so a missing value fails the app at startup.
  • Don't redeclare settings the library owns (PORT, LOG_LEVEL, PROXIED, PROXY_LISTEN_PATH, AUTH_*, AUTH_SSO_*, CONFIG_REMOTE_*, probe and Swagger paths). The full list is in Configuration.
  • When served under an ingress path prefix, set PROXIED=true and PROXY_LISTEN_PATH=/<prefix>.

Secrets:

  • Secrets come from the deployment's secret store (Vault or Kubernetes Secrets, injected as env vars or mounted files). Never put them in git, a conf.py default, .env.example, logs or the image.
  • .env.example lists every variable with a placeholder value and a comment.
  • .env, uv.toml and private keys are git-ignored.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
Every write route's request body has exactly two top-level objects:

{
  "metadata": {
    "project": "payments",
    "space": "net",
    "network": "core",
    "region": "kirya",
    "island": "a1",
    "environment": "prod"
  },
  "spec": {
    "record_name": "api-01",
    "ip": "10.0.0.15",
    "record_type": "A",
    "dns_zone": "net.com"
  }
}
Object Contents metadata Who is asking and where the operation targets: project, space, network, region, island and environment. spec What to do: the resource-specific desired state. It is owned and defined by your API.

docs.title: Metadata rules
docs.text:
1. project is always populated by callers and is required.
  2. space, network, region, island and environment are optional. Use the ones your operation needs. Some APIs need none.
  3. Every API accepts the metadata object, even if it uses none of it. Unused fields are ignored, never rejected.
  4. An API that needs an optional coordinate enforces it in its own schema or operation and returns a 422. It is not made required platform-wide.
  5. Unknown extra keys inside metadata are dropped (Pydantic's default extra="ignore"). Don't set extra="forbid" on metadata models.

docs.title: Base models
docs.text:
From the top-level tashtiot_apis_library package (Schemas):

Base metadata type Validation InfraOperationRequest InfraMetadata: all coordinates optional Live allowlists and coordinate hierarchy from the Config API (Dynamic config validation). Start from this one. RequiredInfraOperationRequest RequiredInfraMetadata: all coordinates required Same validation. Use only if your API needs every coordinate. OperationRequest MetadataRequest: static, no live validation Legacy. Not for new code.

None of these marks only project as required. Every API defines this once, in app/schemas.py, and reuses it:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.config_api import InfraMetadata


class ProjectMetadata(InfraMetadata):
    """Platform metadata: project required, every other coordinate optional."""

    project: str = Field(..., description="The platform application submitting the request")


class MetadataRequest(BaseModel):
    metadata: ProjectMetadata = Field(..., description="Platform metadata (project required).")


# app/v1/dns/schemas.py
class DNSRecordCreate(MetadataRequest):
    spec: DNSRecordCreateSpec

docs.title: Field conventions
docs.text:
• Validate at the boundary. Use typed fields (IPv4Address, Enum, constr, max_length) and field_validators. Bad input fails with 422 before any connector is called.
  • Reuse library building blocks inside spec where they fit: ResourceSpec, NameNamespace, DefaultMetaSpec.
  • For a spec field whose allowed values depend on the request's coordinates, see Constrain a field by resolved config.
  • Every field has a description=.
  • Read and delete routes identify a resource with path or query parameters. Prefer query parameters over a DELETE body, because some proxies drop DELETE bodies.

docs.title: Responses and status codes
docs.text:
• Every route declares response_model= (or a return type annotation). Raw dicts from external services are never passed through.
  • Operation results extend OperationResponse (status, status_code, return_code, stdout), or one of its connector subclasses: AWXOperationResponse (+ job_id) or ArgoOperationResponse (+ app_name). See Architecture.
Situation Code Synchronous read succeeded 200 Synchronous create finished 201 Work accepted, finishing asynchronously (AWX job launched, ArgoCD sync started, job queued) 202 + an id to poll (Long-running work) Delete finished, no body 204 Validation failed 422 (automatic) Missing, invalid or wrong-audience token 401 (automatic, from the middleware) Resource not found 404 Conflict (already exists, concurrent change) 409 An upstream (AWX, ArgoCD, Vault, Git, …) failed 502 An upstream timed out 504 Bug 500 (automatic; never raised deliberately)

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• Connectors raise subclasses of ExternalServiceError: AWXError, ArgoCDError, GitError and VaultError. Each carries service_name, status_code and detail (Errors).
  • ExternalServiceError is a FastAPI HTTPException. Uncaught, it returns the upstream's status code to the client. Routes catch it and return 502: 
    app_name = build_app_name(cluster, namespace, name, "haproxy")
try:
    await create_haproxy_operation(git=git, vault=vault, argocd=argocd, payload=payload.spec)
except ExternalServiceError as err:
    return JSONResponse(
        ArgoOperationResponse(
            app_name=app_name,
            status="Failed",
            status_code=err.status_code,
            stdout=f"{err.service_name}: {err.detail}",
        ).model_dump(),
        status_code=status.HTTP_502_BAD_GATEWAY,
    )
  • An expected upstream 404 (for example "secret doesn't exist yet") is handled in the operation by checking exc.status_code == 404. It is not treated as a failure.
  • Auth error types (AuthConfigError, TokenError, SSOError) are imported from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.errors or the top-level package, never from _internal.
  • Error detail never contains stack traces, tokens, or upstream bodies that may hold secrets.
  • Error bodies use the shape {"detail": "..."}.
  • 422 responses and validation log lines contain only each error's loc, msg and type. The library strips the submitted value (input) and ctx, so a rejected password is never echoed or logged. Custom validator messages must not include the value either: write "not a valid IPv4 address", not f"'{v}' is not a valid IPv4 address".

docs.title: Paths and versioning
docs.text:
• Path scheme: /api/<api-name>/v<N>/<resource>, for example /api/example/v1/dns, set as API_PREFIX in the module's conf.py.
  • Resource names are plural nouns, and HTTP verbs carry the action. Job status: GET .../status/{job_id} or GET .../status?....
  • A breaking change means a new version. It goes in app/v2/<resource>/ alongside v1. Removing or renaming a field, changing a type, or making an optional field required is breaking. Adding an optional field is not.
  • Endpoints are grouped in Swagger with API_TAGS, for example ["v1 - DNS Operations"].
  • Every route has a summary, a description, a response_model and an explicit status code.

docs.title: Router factories
docs.text:
Each module exposes get_<resource>_router(<connectors...>) -> APIRouter. Connectors are captured in the closure and passed explicitly to operations. They are not injected with FastAPI Depends, and they are never constructed per request.

def get_v1_dns_router(awx_client: AWX, provider=None) -> APIRouter:
    router = APIRouter(prefix=config.API_PREFIX, tags=config.API_TAGS)

    @router.post(
        "/",
        response_model=DNSRecordResponse,
        status_code=202,
        summary="Create DNS Record",
        description="Launches the AWX create-DNS job.",
    )
    async def create(record: DNSRecordCreate) -> DNSRecordResponse:
        return await create_dns(record, awx_client, provider)

    return router

docs.title: Async rules
docs.text:
Why these rules exist: Async and the event loop.

  1. Route handlers that do I/O are async def and await async libraries.

  2. Nothing blocks the event loop inside async def code:

    Forbidden Use instead requests.get(...) BaseAPI / httpx.AsyncClient time.sleep(n) await asyncio.sleep(n) subprocess.run(...) await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(...) A sync DB or SDK client Its async driver, or await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...) Heavy CPU work await asyncio.to_thread(...), or move it off the request path (Long-running work)

  3. Plain def handlers are only for trivial CPU-only work (such as /whoami), never as a way to call sync I/O.

  4. Independent calls run concurrently with asyncio.gather.
  5. No asyncio.run() or loop.run_until_complete() inside the app.
  6. Every network await has a timeout. BaseAPI defaults to 10 s, and the connector wait_for_* helpers take explicit timeouts.
  7. Every task created with asyncio.create_task is kept referenced until it finishes (why).

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text:
From the top-level tashtiot_apis_library package (Connectors):

Connector Construct Main async methods AWX AWX(base_url, token) launch_job, launch_workflow_job, get_job_status(job_id, include_logs=False), get_workflow_job_status, wait_for_job_completion(job_id, timeout=300, poll_interval=5), wait_for_workflow_completion, get_job_output(job_id, start_line, page_size) ArgoCD ArgoCD(base_url, api_key, application_set_timeout) sync, create_app, delete_app, get_app_status, wait_for_app_creation, wait_for_app_deletion, wait_for_update, get_app_values/modify_values, get_app_parameters/modify_parameters, add_namespace_to_cluster_secret Git (Bitbucket Server) Git(base_url, token, username_or_email, project_key, repo_slug, default_ref="main", ssh_key_file_path=..., ssh_port=7995) add_file, modify_file, delete_file, get_file_content, file_exists, list_dir, list_files_recursive Vault Vault(base_url, token) read_secret, write_secret, delete_secret BaseAPI (generic) BaseAPI(base_url, headers=None, auth=None, timeout=10.0, verify=False) Any httpx.AsyncClient call

Recipes: Drive AWX, ArgoCD & Vault, Read & write Bitbucket files.

Rules:

  1. Connectors are constructed once in create_app() and injected.
  2. A connector is used instead of raw HTTP whenever one exists. Other services are called through BaseAPI, or through sso_authenticated_api when they need an SSO token.
  3. BaseAPI defaults to verify=False. Services with a valid certificate get verify=True, or REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE/SSL_CERT_FILE pointing at the corporate CA bundle. Turning verification off is a deliberate, commented decision.
  4. Connector results are used as returned (Pydantic models / OperationResponses). Raw JSON isn't parsed by hand.
  5. An AWX launch result (status="successful", status_code=200, job_id) means the job was queued, not finished (AWX is already a job queue).
  6. A new integration that more than one team will use is added to the library as a connector (Add a new connector, Contributing), not copied between APIs.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Design background: Authentication design.

docs.title: Inbound
docs.text:
• Wired by general_create_app(enable_auth=True) and enforced only when AUTH_ENABLED=true. With it off, the app boots open (development only).

  • Exactly one verification mode is configured. Otherwise app creation fails with AuthConfigError.

    Mode Setting Use for JWKS / OIDC (RS256) AUTH_OIDC_ISSUER (discovery) or AUTH_JWKS_URL Production (Secure an API with OIDC & JWKS) Local public key (RS256) AUTH_PUBLIC_KEY_PEM / AUTH_PUBLIC_KEY_PATH Offline or air-gapped verification Shared secret (HS256) AUTH_HS256_SECRET Tests and local development only

  • What is checked: the token's signature, its expiry (AUTH_REQUIRE_EXP=true by default) and its audience. Production sets AUTH_AUDIENCE to the API's audience. AUTH_ISSUER is an optional extra check.

  • The token is read from Authorization: Bearer <jwt> (AUTH_HEADER_NAME). A failure returns 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer.
  • Paths excluded by default: /health, /metrics, /static, /docs, /redoc, /openapi.json, /.well-known, /liveness and /readiness. More can be added with AUTH_EXCLUDE_PATHS. The probes stay excluded.
  • Verified claims are read with Depends(get_current_claims) from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.auth, for logging and auditing.
  • Tokens are verified outside a request with verify_token (Verify a token outside a request).
  • Swagger's Authorize button appears automatically when auth is enforced (OpenAPI & Swagger injection).

Authorization is handled outside the APIs

For now, inbound auth is authentication only: the API checks that the JWT is valid and was issued for its audience. Authorization (which caller may do what, on which project) is enforced outside the APIs. APIs do not add permission checks on token claims such as project, roles or scopes.

docs.title: Outbound (service to service)
docs.text:
• Protected downstream services are called with sso_authenticated_api(base_url) from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.security, which uses the OAuth2 client_credentials grant.
  • It is configured by AUTH_SSO_TOKEN_URL, AUTH_SSO_CLIENT_ID and AUTH_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET (plus the optional SCOPE, AUDIENCE and AUTH_STYLE).
  • Tokens are cached and refreshed by the library. APIs don't cache tokens themselves.
  • On Keycloak, the downstream aud comes from a scope with an Audience mapper (AUTH_SSO_SCOPE).
  • Missing configuration raises AuthConfigError, which the operation catches and turns into a clean error result.
  • Recipes: Call other services with SSO.

docs.title: Remote Config upstream
docs.text: • CONFIG_REMOTE_AUTH_METHOD: sso (default, CONFIG_REMOTE_SSO_*), bearer (CONFIG_REMOTE_BEARER_TOKEN) or none (local dev). See Enable the Remote Config API.

docs.title: Dev tokens
docs.text: • Generated with gen-auth-material (Generate dev auth material, CLI).

docs.title: Remote Config
docs.text:
• Values that vary by environment or coordinate (template ids, endpoints, quotas) are resolved through enable_remote_config_api and provider.resolve_infra_config(payload.metadata), not hard-coded per environment (Enable the Remote Config API).
  • Wiring is opt-in: it is enabled only when CONFIG_API_URL is set, and an AuthConfigError is caught and logged.
  • Every resolved value has a static conf.py default used when the provider is disabled or the key is missing: 
    resolved = await provider.resolve_infra_config(payload.metadata)
template_id = resolved.get("awx_create_dns_template_id", config.AWX_CREATE_DNS_TEMPLATE_ID)

docs.title: Long-running work
docs.text:
Concepts and the decision table: Job queues and long-running work.

  • Work that doesn't finish well within a request (about 5 s) is not awaited in the request.

  • The API contract for such work:

    POST   /api/<api>/v1/<resource>                -> 202 {id, status, ...}
GET    /api/<api>/v1/<resource>/status/{id}    -> 200 {id, status, stdout, ...}

    Statuses use the OperationResponse vocabulary: pending/running while in progress, and successful, failed or canceled when terminal. - The status route returns HTTP 200 whenever it read the job, including a failed one. The job's state goes in the body (status, and for AWX the mapped status_code). It is never copied into the HTTP status. An unknown id returns 404, and an upstream failure returns 502. - AWX jobs are the job queue. An API that launches AWX jobs returns the AWX job_id and reads status with awx.get_job_status. - The library has no job queue implementation. A team that needs a durable queue for work running inside its API implements one or uses an external solution. - In-process background tasks are only for short, best-effort work. Their status comes from the external systems, never from memory, and each task is kept referenced. - Periodic work uses general_create_app(async_background_tasks=[...]) and is idempotent (one copy runs per replica).

docs.title: Multiple replicas
docs.text:
Every API runs as several identical replicas behind a load balancer, and rolling updates run two versions side by side. Why each rule exists: Cloud-native APIs and multiple replicas.

  • Stateless: no source of truth in process memory or on the local filesystem. Any replica must be able to answer any request, so status comes from the owning system (AWX, ArgoCD, Git, Vault) or a shared store.
  • Per-pod caches are allowed only as caches, where a miss refetches.
  • Idempotent and race-tolerant: operations are safe to repeat and safe to run concurrently on two replicas. Cross-replica conflicts are left to the upstream (for example Git add_file on an existing path) and returned as 409. asyncio.Lock is not used as a cross-request guard.
  • Background tasks run on every replica. Only idempotent loops go in async_background_tasks. Work that must run once goes to a Kubernetes CronJob, an AWX schedule or a single-consumer queue.
  • Disposable: the app starts fast and fails fast on bad config. Requests are short enough to finish within the shutdown grace period (30 s by default).
  • Probes: liveness and readiness don't depend on upstream systems.
  • Backward compatible across one release, because old and new pods serve together during a rollout. Breaking changes go to a new API version.
  • One uvicorn process per pod. Scale with replicas.
  • Logs go to stdout with correlation ids. Dashboards aggregate metrics across pods.

docs.title: Multi-step operations
docs.text:
Operations that touch several systems (Git → Vault → ArgoCD) have no distributed transaction. They follow these rules:

  1. Steps are ordered so the cheapest-to-undo step runs first, and nothing user-visible goes live until the last step.
  2. State is snapshotted (the current Git file, the current Vault secret) before it is changed.
  3. On failure, completed steps are compensated in reverse order. Each compensation has its own try/except, and a failed compensation is logged with logger.exception. The original error is then re-raised.
  4. Rollback is symmetric wherever the work continues (inline and in background tasks or jobs).
  5. Operations are idempotent:
    • Create: an existing resource with the same spec returns success or 409 (documented).
    • Update: no-op writes are skipped (example-api compares YAML with yaml_data_equals).
    • Delete: "already gone" (404) counts as success.
  6. Empty secret values are stripped before writing to Vault (filter_secret_payload in example-api).
  7. Resource names are deterministic, derived from the request (for example {cluster}-{namespace}-{resource}-{name}).

docs.title: Logging and observability
docs.text:
Logger setup and level convention: Logging.

  • Logging uses from loguru import logger. Requests and responses are already logged by the library.
  • Use lazy placeholders: logger.info("Syncing app {} in {}", app_name, cluster).
Level Used for debug Payload details (no secrets) info Business events ("launched AWX job 123 for record X") warning Degraded but working error / exception Failures, including stack traces
  • Log lines include correlation identifiers: job_id, app_name, metadata.project and the caller's sub.
  • Never logged: tokens, secrets, Authorization headers, Vault payloads, or request bodies that contain secrets.
  • No print() in application code.
  • /metrics is exposed for Prometheus. Business metrics are added with prometheus_client.
  • /liveness and /readiness stay unauthenticated.
  • The OpenAPI schema (/docs) is the public contract, so summaries, descriptions and examples are kept accurate.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Configuration: asyncio_mode = "auto", pythonpath = ["."], testpaths = ["tests"]. Run with uv run pytest.

Required test Example in example-api Schema validation: valid and invalid payloads (→ 422), including a request with only metadata.project and one with extra metadata keys tests/v1/dns/test_dns_schema.py Routes through TestClient(create_app()) with a valid bearer tests/v1/dns/test_dns_routes.py Auth: no token → 401, bad token → 401, good token → 200 tests/v1/auth_demo/test_auth_demo_routes.py Operations: every failure path, and a check that rollback is invoked — Remote Config fallback (provider disabled or key missing → static default) tests/v1/dns_config/
  • Hermetic environment: the root tests/conftest.py blanks optional AUTH_*/CONFIG_* variables. Module conftests set the required variables before importing app.main.
  • Auth in tests: HS256 (AUTH_ENABLED=true, AUTH_HS256_SECRET=<32+ bytes>), with tokens minted by jwt.encode(...) or gen-auth-material.
  • No real network calls. Mock connector methods with monkeypatch.setattr(...) (mocked async methods are async def), or mock HTTP with respx.
  • Operations take connectors as arguments, so they are unit-tested directly with fakes.

docs.title: Packaging and Docker
docs.text:
• uv sync --group dev installs everything. uv.lock is committed. It is regenerated with uv lock in an environment with full Artifactory access.
  • uv.toml (Artifactory index + credentials) lives in the repo root or ~/.config/uv/uv.toml and is never committed.
  • tashtiot-apis-library is pinned with a minimum version (>=1.1.0). A [tool.uv.sources] path override is for local library development only. Check the Changelog when you bump the version.
  • No new dependency for something the library, the standard library or FastAPI already does. No sync HTTP clients (requests).
  • Dockerfile (follow example-api's):
    • the approved Python 3.12 base image from JFrog Artifactory
    • copy pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .python-version, then run uv sync --frozen --no-dev, then copy app/
    • ARG APP_VERSION / ENV APP_VERSION set from the git tag
    • CMD ["uv","run","--no-sync","-m","app.main","--host","0.0.0.0","--port","5000"]
    • no secrets in the image

docs.title: CI
docs.text:
CI runs on Woodpecker (.woodpecker/*.yaml in each repo) inside the air-gapped network, because it needs the internal JFrog Artifactory and SonarQube.

CI how-to: internal Confluence

The CI how-to and full specification are in the internal Confluence, which is reachable only from the air-gapped network. It defines the pipeline steps, required secrets, images and quality-gate thresholds. Follow it when setting up or changing a pipeline.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
Every API's pipeline does the following:

Step What it checks or produces Tests The pytest suite passes (Testing) Formatting The code matches the formatter (the library itself uses ruff format --check) Linting The linter passes (the library itself uses ruff check) SonarQube The SonarQube scan passes the project's quality gate Build & push The Docker image is built (kaniko) and pushed to JFrog Artifactory, tagged with the release version, which is also passed as APP_VERSION

docs.title: Versioning and changelog (git-cliff)
docs.text:
Releases are versioned with semver (vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH git tags), and both the version and CHANGELOG.md are generated by git-cliff from cliff.toml (see example-api's, or this library's own Changelog for the result).

  • The PR message is the changelog text, not the individual commits. Each merged PR lands on master as one commit carrying the PR's title and description, and that is what git-cliff reads. Commit messages inside a branch are not used.

  • PR titles must be conventional commits, because the prefix decides both the changelog section and the version bump:

    PR title prefix Changelog section Version bump feat: ... Added minor fix: ... Fixed patch refactor: ..., perf: ... Changed patch docs: ... Documentation patch revert: ... Reverted patch build: ..., ci: ... Build, CI patch chore: ..., style: ..., test: ... (not listed) — feat!: ... / fix!: ... or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer (its section) major

    A PR description that mentions security puts the entry under Security.

  • A PR title that isn't a conventional commit is dropped from the changelog and doesn't bump the version (filter_unconventional = true).

  • Write the PR title as the changelog line readers will see, for example feat: add DNS record status endpoint.
  • CHANGELOG.md is committed and generated by git-cliff, so it isn't edited by hand.
  • A breaking API change (a new v<N>, see Paths and versioning) is released as a major version.

docs.title: Known gaps in example-api
docs.text:
example-api is the reference for structure and library usage. Don't copy the following:

docs.title: Pre-merge checklist
docs.text:
Structure and contract

  • [ ] Module follows conf.py / schemas.py / operations.py / routes.py, wired only in create_app().
  • [ ] Every write route accepts {metadata, spec}. metadata.project is required, the other coordinates are optional, and unused metadata is accepted and ignored.
  • [ ] Path is /api/<api>/v<N>/<resource>, and breaking changes went to a new version.
  • [ ] Every route has response_model, summary, description and the correct status code.

Async

  • [ ] No blocking calls in async def (requests, time.sleep, sync clients, heavy CPU work).
  • [ ] Every network await has a timeout. Independent calls use asyncio.gather.
  • [ ] Long work returns 202 + an id (Long-running work). Every created task is referenced.

Connectors and errors

  • [ ] Connectors are built once and injected. No raw HTTP where a connector exists.
  • [ ] ExternalServiceError is mapped to 502. No secrets or stack traces in detail.
  • [ ] Multi-step flows snapshot state, compensate in reverse order, log rollback failures, and are idempotent.
  • [ ] Replica-safe: no state in memory or on local disk, safe under concurrent duplicate requests, no once-only work in async_background_tasks, backward compatible with the previous release.

Security

  • [ ] general_create_app(enable_auth=True). Production configuration uses JWKS/OIDC and sets AUTH_AUDIENCE.
  • [ ] No permission checks on token claims in the API (authorization is handled outside the APIs).
  • [ ] No secrets in git, .env.example, conf.py defaults, logs or the image. TLS verification is on, or turned off with a documented reason.

Quality

  • [ ] .env.example and README.md are updated for every new variable and route.
  • [ ] Tests cover schema (valid, invalid, project-only metadata), routes with auth, failure and rollback paths. No real network calls.
  • [ ] CI is green (tests, formatting, linting, SonarQube) according to the CI how-to in the internal Confluence (CI).
  • [ ] The PR title is a conventional commit that reads well as a changelog line (Versioning and changelog).

A console script (registered as gen-auth-material, also runnable as python -m tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template._internal.security.keygen) that generates an RSA keypair and a signed JWT for exercising local public-key inbound auth.

See Generate dev auth material for task-oriented usage.

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text: By default the command writes jwt_private.pem and jwt_public.pem to the current directory and prints a signed JWT. The minted token has no exp claim and never expires; the verifier requires exp out of the box, so the verifying service must set AUTH_REQUIRE_EXP=false to accept it (the CLI prints this hint). Pass --expires-minutes N to mint a normally-expiring token instead.

The Remote Config capability — an authenticated proxy to an upstream Config API. Import from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.config_api (and the one-call wiring from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template):

docs.title: enable_remote_config_api
docs.text:
enable_remote_config_api(app: FastAPI, *, base_url: str, remote_prefix: str, coordinate_paths: Sequence[str], cache_ttl: int = 60, serve_stale_on_error: bool = False, poll_interval: int = 5, settings: Optional[ConfigRemoteSettings] = None, auth: Optional[Auth] = None, enable_polling: bool = True) -> RemoteConfigProvider

Wire the Remote Config capability onto app and return its provider.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: base_url, remote_prefix: Where the upstream Config API lives and the route prefix under which it serves /projects, /config and /naming. coordinate_paths: Route paths whose coordinate fields get the live enum dropdowns injected. Each entry is a regex string (re.fullmatch against route paths), so a plain path targets exactly itself (["/config", "/naming"]) and a pattern can target a family of routes ([r"/api/v\d+/.*/(config|naming)"]). Not limited to two. settings: Package-side CONFIG_REMOTE_* settings driving the outbound auth method; defaults to a freshly-read ConfigRemoteSettings. auth: Explicit outbound httpx.Auth that overrides settings (escape hatch / tests). When given, settings is not consulted for auth. serve_stale_on_error: When True, an unreachable or 5xx upstream falls back to the last successfully-fetched value for that key (last-known-good, unbounded) instead of raising 502. Defaults to False (preserve the strict 502 contract). enable_polling: Register the background allowlist poller (the task is appended to app.state.async_background_tasks, which general_create_app's lifespan launches at startup). Set False to drive polling yourself.

docs.title: RemoteConfigProvider
docs.text:
RemoteConfigProvider(base_url: str, remote_prefix: str, *, auth: Optional[Auth] = None, timeout: float = 10.0, verify: bool = True, cache_ttl: int = 60, serve_stale_on_error: bool = False)

Resolves config / naming / projects by calling an upstream Config API (same routes) over HTTP, with in-memory caching (cache_ttl-second TTL, default 60s) and the background allowlist-sync loop.

The upstream already performs the cascade merge and naming/registry lookups, so this is a thin authenticated proxy: it forwards the coordinate query parameters and returns the upstream's resolved payload.

Pluggable auth. Outbound requests authenticate via the injected auth (an httpx.Auth), so the caller chooses the method -- client-side SSO (sso_auth(config=...)), a static bearer (StaticBearerAuth), or None for anonymous access. The library's enable_remote_config_api resolves this from the package-side CONFIG_REMOTE_* settings; tests/callers may pass an auth directly.

docs.title: make_config_openapi
docs.text:
make_config_openapi(app: FastAPI, coordinate_paths: Sequence[str]) -> Callable[[], dict]

Build an app.openapi replacement that injects the live allowlists as enum values into the coordinate fields on the routes matched by coordinate_paths -- whether they arrive as query/path parameters or inside a JSON request body.

Each coordinate_paths entry is a regex string matched with re.fullmatch against every route path, so one entry can target a family of routes (r"/api/v\d+/infra/(config|naming)"). A plain path is just a literal regex that matches only itself, so exact-path entries keep working; escape regex metacharacters (., +, ...) if you need them literal. FastAPI path params like {id} are matched literally. An entry that matches no route is a no-op.

This wraps whatever app.openapi is already installed rather than rebuilding the schema from scratch, so it composes with the library's other OpenAPI customizations -- notably the bearer-auth security scheme that general_create_app injects when auth is enabled (the source of Swagger's Authorize button). Replacing app.openapi outright would drop it.

Title/version/openapi_version come from the underlying generator (set on the FastAPI app at construction). The background polling loop nulls app.openapi_schema whenever the allowlists change, so the next schema request regenerates -- through the same wrapped chain -- with current enums.

docs.title: Connectors API

from tashtiot_apis_library import AWX, ArgoCD, Git, Vault

The clients and models are available from each connector's subpackage, e.g. from tashtiot_apis_library.connectors.awx import AWXClient, AWXJob.

See Drive AWX, ArgoCD & Vault and Read & write Bitbucket files for task-oriented usage.

docs.title: Security API (outbound SSO)
docs.text:
The public outbound-SSO surface. Import everything here from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.security:

from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.security import (
    sso_authenticated_api,
    sso_auth,
    get_sso_token_client,
    SSOConfig,
    SSOTokenClient,
    SSOClientCredentialsAuth,
    StaticBearerAuth,
    TokenResponse,
)

See Call other services with SSO for usage.

docs.title: sso_authenticated_api
docs.text:
sso_authenticated_api(base_url: str, *, config: Optional[SSOConfig] = None, settings: Any = None, **base_api_kwargs: Any)

Return a BaseAPI whose every request carries a fresh SSO token.

The connector-style outbound client (async with it for a reusable httpx.AsyncClient) with automatic per-request token injection/refresh:

cfg = SSOConfig(token_url=..., client_id=..., client_secret=..., audience=...)
async with sso_authenticated_api("https://downstream.example.com", config=cfg) as client:
    resp = await client.get("/protected")   # Authorization added & refreshed

Pass config (client-side, preferred) to target a specific identity/audience; omit it to fall back to settings (or the package singleton). Extra keyword args pass through to BaseAPI (e.g. headers, timeout, verify).

docs.title: sso_auth
docs.text:
sso_auth(source: Any = None) -> SSOClientCredentialsAuth

Return an httpx.Auth backed by the shared SSO token client.

source is an SSOConfig, a settings object, or None (package settings) -- see get_sso_token_client.

docs.title: get_sso_token_client
docs.text:
get_sso_token_client(source: Any = None) -> SSOTokenClient

Return a memoized SSOTokenClient for source.

source may be an explicit SSOConfig (client-side config), a settings object exposing AUTH_SSO_* (legacy singleton path), or None to use the package settings. Memoizing by object identity keeps the token cache shared across all callers passing the same object -- so build one SSOConfig per remote and reuse it.

docs.title: SSOConfig
docs.text:
Bases: BaseModel

Client-side OAuth2 client_credentials configuration.

Pass an explicit instance to the SSO helpers (sso_authenticated_api, sso_auth, SSOTokenClient) to mint tokens for a specific identity/audience independently of the package settings singleton -- so a single process can talk to several upstreams that each require a different audience or even a different SSO. Build one instance per remote and reuse it, so its token cache (memoized by object identity) is shared across calls.

The required fields default to None rather than being mandatory so a partially-configured instance still constructs and is validated by SSOTokenClient (which raises a clear AuthConfigError), mirroring the settings-driven path.

SSOTokenClient(config: Any)

Fetches and caches an access token via the client_credentials grant.

Built once per settings object (see get_sso_token_client) so the token cache is shared across callers. Concurrent refreshes are serialised with an asyncio.Lock so a token expiry does not stampede the provider.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Tutorials are learning-oriented: they take you by the hand through a complete, working example so you can get a feel for the library. They don't aim to cover every option — that's what the How-to guides and Reference are for.

Work through them in order:

  1. Your first app — install the library, create a FastAPI app with general_create_app, run it, and explore the batteries that come included (root route, metrics, health probes, Swagger).
  2. Secure your API — generate dev key material, turn on inbound JWT authentication, protect a route, and call it with a token via the Swagger Authorize dialog.

By the end you'll have a running, authenticated service and know where to look when you want to go deeper.

docs.title: Your first app
docs.text: In this tutorial you'll build and run a FastAPI service using the library's application factory, then explore the features it wires up for you out of the box. You need Python ≥ 3.10 and about five minutes.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
pip install tashtiot-apis-library
# uvicorn comes as a dependency; install nothing else for this tutorial

docs.title: 2. Create the app
docs.text:
The factory general_create_app() returns a fully-configured FastAPI instance. Create a file called main.py:

from tashtiot_apis_library import general_create_app
from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.utils import settings

app = general_create_app()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn

    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=settings.PORT)

That's the whole app. general_create_app() has already registered logging/timing middleware, an exception handler, a root route, a Prometheus metrics endpoint, health probes, and a self-hosted Swagger UI.

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text:
python main.py
# or: uvicorn main:app --port 8000

You should see structured Loguru output on stdout as the app starts.

docs.title: 4. Explore what you got
docs.text:
With the server running, open these in a browser or with curl:

URL What it is http://localhost:8000/ The built-in root route http://localhost:8000/docs Swagger UI (served from bundled static assets) http://localhost:8000/redoc ReDoc http://localhost:8000/metrics Prometheus-format metrics http://localhost:8000/health/live Liveness probe (Kubernetes-ready) http://localhost:8000/health/ready Readiness probe

Each request is logged with its method, path, and processing time.

docs.title: 5. Add your own route
docs.text:
The returned app is an ordinary FastAPI instance — add routes the usual way:

@app.get("/hello")
def hello():
    return {"message": "hello from tashtiot-apis-library"}

Restart and visit http://localhost:8000/hello. It shows up in /docs automatically.

docs.title: 6. Configure via environment
docs.text:
Every built-in is configurable through environment variables (or a .env file). For example, to change the port and log level:

PORT=9000
LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG
APP_NAME=MyFirstApp

See the full list in the Configuration reference.

  • How-to guides — connect to ArgoCD/AWX/Vault, call services with SSO, and more.
  • Architecture — understand how the factory and connectors are structured.

docs.title: Secure your API
docs.text: In this tutorial you'll add inbound JWT authentication to the app from Your first app: mint a dev key + token, turn auth on, protect a route, and call it with a bearer token through Swagger. We'll use local public-key mode because it needs no external identity provider — perfect for learning.

docs.title: 1. Generate dev key material
docs.text:
The package installs a gen-auth-material command. Run it to create an RSA keypair and a signed token:

gen-auth-material

This writes jwt_private.pem and jwt_public.pem to the current directory and prints a JWT plus a hint. By default the token has no exp claim and never expires — convenient for a tutorial.

Non-expiring tokens

Because the minted token has no exp, the verifier must be told to accept it. We do that below with AUTH_REQUIRE_EXP=false. To mint a normally-expiring token instead, pass --expires-minutes 30. See the CLI reference.

docs.title: 2. Turn auth on
docs.text:
Authentication is dual-gated: it activates only when you both pass enable_auth=True in code and set AUTH_ENABLED=true in the environment. This makes it impossible to ship auth-on code that silently runs auth-off (or vice versa).

Update main.py:

from fastapi import Depends
from tashtiot_apis_library import general_create_app
from tashtiot_apis_library.fastapi_template.auth import get_current_claims

app = general_create_app(enable_auth=True)  # gate 1: the code flag


@app.get("/me")
def me(claims: dict = Depends(get_current_claims)):
    return claims

get_current_claims is a FastAPI dependency that returns the verified JWT claims (the auth middleware put them on request.state.user), or raises 401 if the request wasn't authenticated.

docs.title: 3. Point the verifier at your public key
docs.text:
Create a .env file next to main.py:

AUTH_ENABLED=true                 # gate 2: the runtime switch
AUTH_PUBLIC_KEY_PATH=jwt_public.pem
AUTH_REQUIRE_EXP=false            # accept the non-expiring dev token from step 1

The verifier auto-selects its mode from whatever material you configure — here a public key file selects offline RS256 verification. (Set exactly one material; see Authentication design.)

docs.title: 4. Run and try it
docs.text:
python main.py

Call the protected route without a token — you get a 401:

curl -i http://localhost:8000/me
# HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized

Now pass the token printed in step 1:

TOKEN="<paste the token from gen-auth-material>"
curl -s http://localhost:8000/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# {"sub": "local-dev", ...}

docs.title: 5. Use the Swagger Authorize button
docs.text: Because auth is active, Swagger UI gains an Authorize button. Open http://localhost:8000/docs, click Authorize, paste the token, and use Try it out on /me — the request now carries your bearer token.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• Auth is dual-gated (enable_auth=True + AUTH_ENABLED=true).
  • The verifier picks its mode from the configured material (here, a local public key).
  • Routes read the verified identity via Depends(get_current_claims).
